    Continued Fractions

    Introduction

    A continued fraction represents a real number as the limit of a sequence of convergent rational numbers. The rational numbers in this sequence are easy to compute and provide the best approximations to the real number, which is why continued fractions are often used in algorithm competitions. In addition, continued fractions are closely related to the Euclidean algorithm, and thus can be applied to a series of number theory problems.

    About the algorithm implementations for continued fractions

    This article will provide several continued fraction algorithm implementations, some of which may not guarantee that all integers involved in the intermediate computation process fall within the range of 32-bit or 64-bit integer variables. For such cases, please refer to the corresponding Python implementation, or replace the integer variables in the C++ implementation with high-precision integer types. To highlight the key points, some code in this article may call functions implemented earlier without repeating the implementation.

    Continued Fractions

    A continued fraction is itself merely a formal notation.

    Finite continued fraction

    For a sequence {𝑎𝑘}𝑛𝑖=0{ak}i=0n, the continued fraction [𝑎0,𝑎1,⋯,𝑎𝑛][a0,a1,⋯,an] represents the expansion

    𝑥=𝑎0+1𝑎1+1𝑎2+1⋯+1𝑎𝑛.x=a0+1a1+1a2+1⋯+1an.

    The continued fraction is meaningful if and only if the corresponding expansion is meaningful. These 𝑎𝑘ak are called the terms or coefficients of the continued fraction.

    Notation

    More general continued fractions allow the numerators in the expansion not to be always 1, and the corresponding continued fraction notation also needs to be modified, which is beyond the scope of this article. Also, in some literature, the first comma ",," may be written as a semicolon ";;", which does not differ in meaning from the notation in this article.

    Of course, continued fractions can also be extended to the case of infinite sequences.

    Infinite continued fraction

    For an infinite sequence {𝑎𝑘}∞𝑖=0{ak}i=0∞, the continued fraction [𝑎0,𝑎1,⋯][a0,a1,⋯] represents the limit

    𝑥=lim𝑘→∞𝑥𝑘=lim𝑘→∞[𝑎0,𝑎1,⋯,𝑎𝑘].x=limk→∞xk=limk→∞[a0,a1,⋯,ak].

    The continued fraction is meaningful if and only if the corresponding limit is meaningful. Here, 𝑥𝑘 =[𝑎0,𝑎1,⋯,𝑎𝑘]xk=[a0,a1,⋯,ak] is called the 𝑘k-th convergent of 𝑥x, and 𝑟𝑘 =[𝑎𝑘,𝑎𝑘+1,⋯]rk=[ak,ak+1,⋯] is called the 𝑘k-th remainder or complete quotient of 𝑥x. Accordingly, the term 𝑎𝑘ak is sometimes also called the 𝑘k-th partial quotient.

    Simple Continued Fractions

    In number theory, we mainly consider continued fractions where all terms are integers.

    Simple continued fraction

    For a continued fraction [𝑎0,𝑎1,⋯][a0,a1,⋯], if 𝑎0a0 is an integer and 𝑎1,𝑎2,⋯a1,a2,⋯ are all positive integers, then it is called a simple continued fraction, also simply called a continued fraction. If the sequence {𝑎𝑖}{ai} is finite, it is called a finite (simple) continued fraction; otherwise, it is called an infinite (simple) continued fraction. Moreover, 𝑎0a0 is called its integer part.

    Unless otherwise specified, continued fractions in this article refer to simple continued fractions. It can be proved that infinite simple continued fractions are necessarily convergent, and the remainders of simple continued fractions are also necessarily positive.

    Continued fractions have the following basic properties:

    Properties

    Let 𝑥 =[𝑎0,𝑎1,𝑎2,⋯]x=[a0,a1,a2,⋯]. Then the following properties hold:

    1. For any 𝑘 ∈𝐙k∈Z, we have 𝑥 +𝑘 =[𝑎0 +𝑘,𝑎1,𝑎2,⋯]x+k=[a0+k,a1,a2,⋯];
    2. For a real number 𝑥 >1x>1, we have 𝑎0 >0a0>0, and its reciprocal 𝑥−1 =[0,𝑎0,𝑎1,𝑎2,⋯]x−1=[0,a0,a1,a2,⋯].

    Finite continued fractions correspond to rational numbers. Every rational number can be represented as a continued fraction in exactly two ways, with lengths necessarily odd and even. The only difference between these two representations is whether the last term is 11, i.e.,

    𝑥=[𝑎0,𝑎1,⋯,𝑎𝑛]=[𝑎0,𝑎1,⋯,𝑎𝑛−1,1].x=[a0,a1,⋯,an]=[a0,a1,⋯,an−1,1].

    These two continued fractions are called the continued fraction representations of the rational number 𝑥x. Among them, the one with the last term not equal to 11 is called the standard representation, and the one with the last term equal to 11 is called the non-standard representation.1

    Example

    The continued fraction representation of the rational number 𝑥 =53x=53 is

    𝑥=[1,1,1,1]=1+11+11+11,𝑥=[1,1,2]=1+11+12.x=[1,1,1,1]=1+11+11+11,x=[1,1,2]=1+11+12.

    Infinite continued fractions correspond to irrational numbers. Moreover, every irrational number can be represented as a continued fraction in exactly one way, which is called the continued fraction representation of the irrational number.

    Computing the Continued Fraction Representation

    To find the continued fraction representation of a real number 𝑥x, one only needs to note that if its remainder 𝑟𝑘rk is not an integer, it must satisfy

    𝑟𝑘=[𝑎𝑘,𝑎𝑘+1,⋯]=[𝑎𝑘,𝑟𝑘+1]=𝑎𝑘+1𝑟𝑘+1.rk=[ak,ak+1,⋯]=[ak,rk+1]=ak+1rk+1.

    Moreover, 𝑟𝑘+1 >1rk+1>1. Therefore, we can recursively compute starting from 𝑟0 =𝑥r0=x

    𝑎𝑘=⌊𝑟𝑘⌋, 𝑟𝑘+1=1𝑟𝑘−𝑎𝑘.ak=⌊rk⌋, rk+1=1rk−ak.

    The sequence {𝑎𝑘}{ak} generated by this process is always uniquely determined, unless some remainder 𝑟𝑘rk becomes an integer. If 𝑟𝑘rk becomes an integer, the process should terminate, and we can choose to output either the standard representation or the non-standard representation.

    In algorithm competitions, we often deal with rational numbers 𝑥 =𝑝𝑞x=pq. In this case, each remainder 𝑟𝑘rk is a rational number 𝑝𝑘𝑞𝑘pkqk, and for 𝑘 >0k>0, since 𝑟𝑘 >1rk>1, we always have 𝑝𝑘 >𝑞𝑘pk>qk. Computing the recurrence relation, we can discover that

    𝑎𝑘=⌊𝑝𝑘𝑞𝑘⌋, 𝑟𝑘+1=1𝑟𝑘−𝑎𝑘=𝑞𝑘𝑝𝑘−𝑎𝑘𝑞𝑘=𝑞𝑘𝑝𝑘mod𝑞𝑘.ak=⌊pkqk⌋, rk+1=1rk−ak=qkpk−akqk=qkpkmodqk.

    This computation process is actually the Euclidean algorithm performed on 𝑝p and 𝑞q. This also shows that for a rational number 𝑟 =𝑝𝑞r=pq, the length of the continued fraction representation is 𝑂(log⁡min{𝑝,𝑞})O(log⁡min{p,q}). The complexity of computing the continued fraction representation of 𝑝𝑞pq is also 𝑂(log⁡min{𝑝,𝑞})O(log⁡min{p,q}).

    Reference implementation

    Given the numerator 𝑝p and denominator 𝑞q of a fraction, output the continued fraction coefficient sequence [𝑎0,𝑎1,⋯,𝑎𝑛][a0,a1,⋯,an].

    1
2

7
8

    // Find the continued fraction representation of P/Q.
auto fraction(int p, int q) {
  std::vector<int> a;
  while (q) {
    a.push_back(p / q);
    std::tie(p, q) = std::make_pair(q, p % q);
  }
  return a;
}

    # Find the continued fraction representation of P/Q.
def fraction(p, q):
    a = []
    while q:
        a.append(p // q)
        p, q = q, p % q
    return a

    Convergents

    The concept of convergents was introduced in the definition of continued fractions. The convergents of a real number are the convergents of its continued fraction representation: in the continued fraction representation of a real number 𝑥x, keeping only the first 𝑘k terms, the obtained continued fraction 𝑥𝑘xk is called the 𝑘k-th convergent of the real number 𝑥x. The convergents 𝑥𝑘xk of a real number 𝑥x are all rational numbers, and the sequence {𝑥𝑘}{xk} converges to the real number 𝑥x.

    Example: Convergents of the golden ratio

    The first few convergents of the continued fraction 𝑥 =[1,1,1,1,⋯]x=[1,1,1,1,⋯] are

    𝑥0=[1]=1,𝑥1=[1,1]=2,𝑥2=[1,1,1]=32,𝑥3=[1,1,1,1]=53,𝑥4=[1,1,1,1,1]=85.x0=[1]=1,x1=[1,1]=2,x2=[1,1,1]=32,x3=[1,1,1,1]=53,x4=[1,1,1,1,1]=85.

    It can be proved by induction that

    𝑥𝑘=𝐹𝑘+2𝐹𝑘+1,xk=Fk+2Fk+1,

    where {𝐹𝑘}{Fk} is the Fibonacci sequence. According to its general term formula,

    𝑥𝑘=𝜙𝑘+2−(−𝜙)−(𝑘+2)𝜙𝑘+1−(−𝜙)−(𝑘+1),xk=ϕk+2−(−ϕ)−(k+2)ϕk+1−(−ϕ)−(k+1),

    where 𝜙 =1+√52ϕ=1+52 is the golden ratio. As 𝑘k tends to infinity,

    𝑥=lim𝑘→∞𝑥𝑘=𝜙.x=limk→∞xk=ϕ.

    Therefore, the continued fraction 𝑥 =[1,1,1,1,⋯]x=[1,1,1,1,⋯] represents the golden ratio 𝜙ϕ.

    These convergents approach the corresponding real numbers, so they can be used to approximate the real numbers. For this purpose, it is necessary to understand the properties of convergents.

    Recurrence Relations

    First, we need to solve the computation problem of these convergents. Although convergents are always obtained by adding one term to the continued fraction, we do not need to recompute its value each time. In fact, convergents have the following recurrence relations:

    Recurrence formula

    For the continued fraction 𝑥 =[𝑎0,𝑎1,𝑎2,⋯]x=[a0,a1,a2,⋯], let its 𝑘k-th convergent 𝑥𝑘xk be written as the fraction 𝑝𝑘𝑞𝑘pkqk. Then we have

    𝑝𝑘=𝑎𝑘𝑝𝑘−1+𝑝𝑘−2,𝑞𝑘=𝑎𝑘𝑞𝑘−1+𝑞𝑘−2.pk=akpk−1+pk−2,qk=akqk−1+qk−2.

    The starting point of the recurrence is the (formal) fractions

    𝑥−1=𝑝−1𝑞−1=10, 𝑥−2=𝑝−2𝑞−2=01.x−1=p−1q−1=10, x−2=p−2q−2=01.
    Proof

    The numerator and denominator of the convergent 𝑥𝑘xk can be regarded as multivariate polynomials in 𝑎0,𝑎1,⋯,𝑎𝑘a0,a1,⋯,ak:

    𝑟𝑘=𝑃𝑘(𝑎0,𝑎1,⋯,𝑎𝑘)𝑄𝑘(𝑎0,𝑎1,⋯,𝑎𝑘).rk=Pk(a0,a1,⋯,ak)Qk(a0,a1,⋯,ak).

    According to the definition of convergents,

    𝑟𝑘=𝑎0+1[𝑎1,𝑎2,⋯,𝑎𝑘]=𝑎0+𝑄𝑘−1(𝑎1,⋯,𝑎𝑘)𝑃𝑘−1(𝑎1,⋯,𝑎𝑘)=𝑎0𝑃𝑘−1(𝑎1,…,𝑎𝑘)+𝑄𝑘−1(𝑎1,⋯,𝑎𝑘)𝑃𝑘−1(𝑎1,⋯,𝑎𝑘).rk=a0+1[a1,a2,⋯,ak]=a0+Qk−1(a1,⋯,ak)Pk−1(a1,⋯,ak)=a0Pk−1(a1,…,ak)+Qk−1(a1,⋯,ak)Pk−1(a1,⋯,ak).

    Comparing with the above equation, if we set 𝑄𝑘(𝑎0,⋯,𝑎𝑘) =𝑃𝑘−1(𝑎1,⋯,𝑎𝑘)Qk(a0,⋯,ak)=Pk−1(a1,⋯,ak), then the convergent can be written as

    𝑟𝑘=𝑃𝑘(𝑎0,𝑎1,⋯,𝑎𝑘)𝑃𝑘−1(𝑎1,⋯,𝑎𝑘)rk=Pk(a0,a1,⋯,ak)Pk−1(a1,⋯,ak)

    and the polynomial 𝑃𝑘Pk satisfies the recurrence relation

    𝑃𝑘(𝑎0,⋯,𝑎𝑘)=𝑎0𝑃𝑘−1(𝑎1,⋯,𝑎𝑘)+𝑃𝑘−2(𝑎2,⋯,𝑎𝑘).Pk(a0,⋯,ak)=a0Pk−1(a1,⋯,ak)+Pk−2(a2,⋯,ak).

    Because

    𝑟0=𝑎0, 𝑟1=𝑎0+1𝑎1=𝑎0𝑎1+1𝑎1,r0=a0, r1=a0+1a1=a0a1+1a1,

    the starting point of the recurrence is

    𝑃0(𝑎0)=𝑎0, 𝑃1(𝑎0,𝑎1)=𝑎0𝑎1+1.P0(a0)=a0, P1(a0,a1)=a0a1+1.

    If we set

    𝑃−1=1, 𝑃−2=0,P−1=1, P−2=0,

    we can verify that the above recurrence relation also holds for 𝑘 =0,1k=0,1. This is equivalent to specifying the formal fractions 𝑟−1 =10r−1=10 and 𝑟−2 =01r−2=01.

    The sequence of polynomials 𝑃𝑘Pk satisfying the above recurrence relation is called the continuant3. It can be written in the form of a determinant:

    𝑃𝑘(𝑎0,⋯,𝑎𝑘)=det⁡⎛⎜ ⎜ ⎜ ⎜ ⎜ ⎜ ⎜ ⎜ ⎜ ⎜⎝𝑎010⋯0−1𝑎11⋱⋮0−1𝑎2⋱0⋮⋱⋱⋱10⋯0−1𝑎𝑘⎞⎟ ⎟ ⎟ ⎟ ⎟ ⎟ ⎟ ⎟ ⎟ ⎟⎠.Pk(a0,⋯,ak)=det⁡(a010⋯0−1a11⋱⋮0−1a2⋱0⋮⋱⋱⋱10⋯0−1ak).

    This is the determinant of a tridiagonal matrix. Expanding from the upper left corner, we can verify that it has the above recurrence relation and initial conditions. Conversely, expanding from the lower right corner, we obtain the recurrence relation

    𝑃𝑘(𝑎0,⋯,𝑎𝑘)=𝑎𝑘𝑃𝑘−1(𝑎0,⋯,𝑎𝑘−1)+𝑃𝑘−2(𝑎0,⋯,𝑎𝑘−2),Pk(a0,⋯,ak)=akPk−1(a0,⋯,ak−1)+Pk−2(a0,⋯,ak−2),

    which is what we wanted to prove.

    Notation

    When this article writes the convergent 𝑥𝑘xk as 𝑝𝑘𝑞𝑘pkqk, it is always understood that the numerator 𝑝𝑘pk and denominator 𝑞𝑘qk are given by the above recurrence relation. Below, we will also show that this always gives the reduced form of the convergents.

    This recurrence formula shows that

    𝑥𝑘=𝑎𝑘𝑝𝑘−1+𝑝𝑘−2𝑎𝑘𝑞𝑘−1+𝑞𝑘−2xk=akpk−1+pk−2akqk−1+qk−2

    lies between 𝑥𝑘−1xk−1 and 𝑥𝑘−2xk−2.

    As corollaries of the recurrence relation for convergents, the reverse order theorem and reciprocal theorem hold:

    Reverse order theorem

    Let the 𝑘k-th convergent of the real number 𝑥 =[𝑎0,𝑎1,𝑎2,⋯]x=[a0,a1,a2,⋯] be 𝑝𝑘𝑞𝑘pkqk. Then the ratios of numerators and denominators of consecutive convergents are respectively

    𝑝𝑘𝑝𝑘−1=[𝑎𝑘,𝑎𝑘−1,⋯,𝑎1,𝑎0],𝑞𝑘𝑞𝑘−1=[𝑎𝑘,𝑎𝑘−1,⋯,𝑎1].pkpk−1=[ak,ak−1,⋯,a1,a0],qkqk−1=[ak,ak−1,⋯,a1].

    If 𝑎0 =0a0=0, then the first continued fraction should be understood as truncated at the second-to-last term, i.e., [𝑎𝑘,𝑎𝑘−1,⋯,𝑎2][ak,ak−1,⋯,a2].

    Proof

    In the recurrence relations for 𝑝𝑘pk and 𝑞𝑘qk, dividing both sides by 𝑝𝑘−1pk−1 and 𝑞𝑘−1qk−1 respectively, we obtain

    𝑝𝑘𝑝𝑘−1=𝑎𝑘+𝑝𝑘−2𝑝𝑘−1,𝑞𝑘𝑞𝑘−1=𝑎𝑘+𝑞𝑘−2𝑞𝑘−1.pkpk−1=ak+pk−2pk−1,qkqk−1=ak+qk−2qk−1.

    Iterating these two equations, we obtain two continued fractions. Then substituting the initial values 𝑝0𝑝−1 =𝑎0p0p−1=a0 and 𝑞1𝑞0 =𝑎1q1q0=a1. For the case 𝑎0 =0a0=0, if we understand the obtained continued fraction as a formal expression, then its remainder

    [𝑎2,𝑎1,0]=𝑎2+1𝑎1+10=𝑎2+00𝑎1+1=𝑎2.[a2,a1,0]=a2+1a1+10=a2+00a1+1=a2.

    Therefore, the last two terms can be omitted directly. For a strict proof, one only needs to note that this equation can be seen as the limit as 𝑎0 →0a0→0.

    Reciprocal theorem

    The reciprocals of the convergents of a real number 𝑥 >0x>0 are the convergents of 𝑥−1x−1.

    Proof

    Let 𝑥 >1x>1 have the continued fraction representation [𝑎0,𝑎1,𝑎2,⋯][a0,a1,a2,⋯], then the continued fraction representation of 𝑥−1x−1 is [0,𝑎0,𝑎1,𝑎2,⋯][0,a0,a1,a2,⋯]. Their convergents can be obtained from the recurrence relations. Moreover, for 𝑥x, we have initial conditions 𝑥−2 =01x−2=01 and 𝑥−1 =10x−1=10; for 𝑦 =𝑥−1y=x−1, we have initial conditions 𝑦−1 =10y−1=10 and 𝑦0 =01y0=01. Therefore, we have 𝑥−2 =(𝑦−1)−1x−2=(y−1)−1 and 𝑥−1 =(𝑦0)−1x−1=(y0)−1. From the recurrence relation, we obtain 𝑥𝑘 =𝑦−1𝑘+1xk=yk+1−1. This shows that the reciprocals of the convergents of 𝑥x are the convergents of 𝑦 =𝑥−1y=x−1. For the case 0 <𝑥 ≤10<x≤1, a similar discussion can be made.

    Using the recurrence relation obtained in this section, we can derive the following algorithm for computing convergents:

    Reference implementation

    Given the continued fraction coefficients 𝑎0,𝑎1,⋯,𝑎𝑛a0,a1,⋯,an, find the sequences of numerators and denominators of convergents (𝑝0,𝑞0),(𝑝1,𝑞1),⋯,(𝑝𝑛,𝑞𝑛)(p0,q0),(p1,q1),⋯,(pn,qn).

    // Find the convergents of a continued fraction A.
// Numerators and denominators stored separately in P and Q.
auto convergents(std::vector<int> a) {
  std::vector<int> p = {0, 1};
  std::vector<int> q = {1, 0};
  for (auto it : a) {
    p.push_back(p.back() * it + p.end()[-2]);
    q.push_back(q.back() * it + q.end()[-2]);
  }
  return std::make_pair(p, q);
}

    # Find the convergents of a continued fraction A.
# Numerators and denominators stored separately in P and Q.
def convergents(a):
    p = [0, 1]
    q = [1, 0]
    for it in a:
        p.append(p[-1] * it + p[-2])
        q.append(q[-1] * it + q[-2])
    return p, q

    Error Estimation

    Using the recurrence formula for convergents, we can estimate the error generated when approximating a real number with convergents.

    First, we can compute the difference between consecutive convergents:

    Difference of convergents

    Let 𝑥𝑘 =𝑝𝑘𝑞𝑘xk=pkqk be the 𝑘k-th convergent of the real number 𝑥x. Then we have

    𝑝𝑘+1𝑞𝑘−𝑝𝑘𝑞𝑘+1=(−1)𝑘.pk+1qk−pkqk+1=(−1)k.

    Therefore, the difference between consecutive convergents is

    𝑥𝑘+1−𝑥𝑘=(−1)𝑘𝑞𝑘+1𝑞𝑘.xk+1−xk=(−1)kqk+1qk.
    Proof

    According to the recurrence relation, we have

    det⁡(𝑝𝑘+1𝑝𝑘𝑞𝑘+1𝑞𝑘)=det⁡(𝑎𝑘+1𝑝𝑘+𝑝𝑘−1𝑝𝑘𝑎𝑘+1𝑞𝑘+𝑞𝑘−1𝑞𝑘)=det⁡(𝑝𝑘−1𝑝𝑘𝑞𝑘−1𝑞𝑘)=−det⁡(𝑝𝑘𝑝𝑘−1𝑞𝑘𝑞𝑘−1)=(−1)𝑘+2det⁡(1001)=(−1)𝑘.det⁡(pk+1pkqk+1qk)=det⁡(ak+1pk+pk−1pkak+1qk+qk−1qk)=det⁡(pk−1pkqk−1qk)=−det⁡(pkpk−1qkqk−1)=(−1)k+2det⁡(1001)=(−1)k.

    This is 𝑝𝑘+1𝑞𝑘 −𝑝𝑘𝑞𝑘+1 =( −1)𝑘pk+1qk−pkqk+1=(−1)k. Dividing both sides by 𝑞𝑘+1𝑞𝑘qk+1qk, we obtain the conclusion about 𝑥𝑘+1 −𝑥𝑘xk+1−xk.

    Therefore, odd-indexed convergents are always greater than the adjacent terms, and even-indexed convergents are always less than the adjacent terms: convergents alternate.

    If we only consider even-indexed (odd-indexed) convergents, the sequence is also monotonically increasing (decreasing). This is because

    𝑥𝑘+2−𝑥𝑘=(−1)𝑘+1𝑞𝑘+2𝑞𝑘+1+(−1)𝑘𝑞𝑘+1𝑞𝑘=(−1)𝑘(𝑞𝑘+2−𝑞𝑘)𝑞𝑘+2𝑞𝑘+1𝑞𝑘=(−1)𝑘𝑎𝑘+2𝑞𝑘+2𝑞𝑘xk+2−xk=(−1)k+1qk+2qk+1+(−1)kqk+1qk=(−1)k(qk+2−qk)qk+2qk+1qk=(−1)kak+2qk+2qk

    which is positive (negative) when 𝑘k is even (odd). At the same time, because the recurrence relation 𝑞𝑘 =𝑎𝑘𝑞𝑘−1 +𝑞𝑘−2qk=akqk−1+qk−2 holds, the growth rate of denominators 𝑞𝑘qk is no slower than that of the Fibonacci sequence. Therefore, the difference between consecutive terms must tend to zero. This shows that even-indexed and odd-indexed convergents approach the same limit from below and above respectively. This proves that infinite simple continued fractions must converge. The dynamics of convergents approaching the corresponding real number can be seen in the following figure:

    Upper (lower) convergent

    For a real number 𝑥x and its convergent 𝑥𝑘xk, if 𝑥𝑘 >𝑥xk>x (𝑥𝑘 <𝑥xk<x), then 𝑥𝑘xk is called the upper (lower) convergent of 𝑥x.

    As explained earlier, upper convergents are odd-indexed convergents, and lower convergents are even-indexed convergents.

    Using the difference formula, we can express the real number 𝑥x as an alternating series:

    𝑥=𝑎0+∞∑𝑘=0(−1)𝑘𝑞𝑘+1𝑞𝑘.x=a0+∑k=0∞(−1)kqk+1qk.

    The convergents and remainders in the continued fraction definition are respectively the partial sums and remainders of this series.

    Using the difference formula, we can also directly estimate the error in approximating a real number with convergents:

    Error

    Let 𝑥𝑘 =𝑝𝑘𝑞𝑘 ≠𝑥xk=pkqk≠x be the 𝑘k-th convergent of the real number 𝑥x. Then we have

    𝑥𝑘−𝑥=(−1)𝑘𝑞𝑘(𝑟𝑘+1𝑞𝑘+𝑞𝑘−1),xk−x=(−1)kqk(rk+1qk+qk−1),

    where 𝑟𝑘+1rk+1 is the (𝑘 +1)(k+1)-th remainder of the real number 𝑥x. Furthermore, we have

    12𝑞2𝑘+1≤1𝑞𝑘(𝑞𝑘+𝑞𝑘+1)≤∣𝑥−𝑝𝑘𝑞𝑘∣≤1𝑞𝑘𝑞𝑘+1≤1𝑞2𝑘.12qk+12≤1qk(qk+qk+1)≤|x−pkqk|≤1qkqk+1≤1qk2.
    Proof

    Since 𝑥 =[𝑎0,𝑎1,⋯,𝑎𝑘,𝑟𝑘+1]x=[a0,a1,⋯,ak,rk+1], and the difference formula for convergents also holds for formal continued fractions, we have

    𝑥−𝑥𝑘=(−1)𝑘𝑞𝑘(𝑟𝑘+1𝑞𝑘+𝑞𝑘−1),x−xk=(−1)kqk(rk+1qk+qk−1),

    where 𝑟𝑘+1𝑞𝑘 +𝑞𝑘−1rk+1qk+qk−1 is the denominator of the (𝑘 +1)(k+1)-th convergent of this formal continued fraction obtained according to the recurrence formula.

    To complete the inequality estimation, we only need to note that when 𝑥𝑘 ≠𝑥xk≠x, we always have

    1≤𝑎𝑘+1≤𝑟𝑘+1≤𝑎𝑘+1+1,1≤ak+1≤rk+1≤ak+1+1,

    so we have

    𝑞𝑘+1=𝑎𝑘+1𝑞𝑘+𝑞𝑘−1≤𝑟𝑘+1𝑞𝑘+𝑞𝑘−1≤𝑞𝑘+(𝑎𝑘+1𝑞𝑘+𝑞𝑘−1)=𝑞𝑘+𝑞𝑘+1.qk+1=ak+1qk+qk−1≤rk+1qk+qk−1≤qk+(ak+1qk+qk−1)=qk+qk+1.

    Therefore, we have the inequality

    1𝑞𝑘(𝑞𝑘+𝑞𝑘+1)≤∣𝑥−𝑝𝑘𝑞𝑘∣=1𝑞𝑘(𝑟𝑘+1𝑞𝑘+𝑞𝑘−1)≤1𝑞𝑘𝑞𝑘+1.1qk(qk+qk+1)≤|x−pkqk|=1qk(rk+1qk+qk−1)≤1qkqk+1.

    To get the outer bounds, we only need to note that 𝑞𝑘 ≤𝑞𝑘+1qk≤qk+1.

    A simple corollary of the difference formula in this section is: all convergents 𝑝𝑘𝑞𝑘pkqk are reduced.

    Corollary

    For any real number 𝑥x, and the convergent 𝑥𝑘 =𝑝𝑘𝑞𝑘xk=pkqk whose numerator and denominator are given by the recurrence formula, then 𝑝𝑘𝑞𝑘pkqk is a reduced fraction, i.e., gcd(𝑝𝑘,𝑞𝑘) =1gcd(pk,qk)=1.

    Proof

    Apply the Bézout's theorem to the difference formula.

    In fact, solutions to linear Diophantine equations in two variables can be solved using continued fractions.

    Solving linear Diophantine equations in two variables

    Given 𝐴,𝐵,𝐶 ∈𝐙A,B,C∈Z. Find 𝑥,𝑦 ∈𝐙x,y∈Z such that 𝐴𝑥 +𝐵𝑦 =𝐶Ax+By=C holds.

    Solution

    Although this problem is usually solved using the extended Euclidean algorithm, it can also be solved using continued fractions.

    Let 𝐴𝐵 =[𝑎0,𝑎1,⋯,𝑎𝑘]AB=[a0,a1,⋯,ak]. Above, we proved 𝑝𝑘𝑞𝑘−1 −𝑝𝑘−1𝑞𝑘 =( −1)𝑘−1pkqk−1−pk−1qk=(−1)k−1. Substituting 𝑝𝑘pk and 𝑞𝑘qk with 𝐴A and 𝐵B, we obtain

    𝐴𝑞𝑘−1−𝐵𝑝𝑘−1=(−1)𝑘−1𝑔,Aqk−1−Bpk−1=(−1)k−1g,

    where 𝑔 =gcd(𝐴,𝐵)g=gcd(A,B). If 𝑔g divides 𝐶C, then one solution is 𝑥 =( −1)𝑘−1𝐶𝑔𝑞𝑘−1x=(−1)k−1Cgqk−1 and 𝑦 =( −1)𝑘𝐶𝑔𝑝𝑘−1y=(−1)kCgpk−1; otherwise there is no solution.

    // Return (x,y) such that Ax+By=C.
// Assume that such (x,y) exists.
auto dio(int A, int B, int C) {
  std::vector<int> p, q;
  std::tie(p, q) = convergents(fraction(A, B));
  C /= A / p.back();
  int t = p.size() % 2 ? -1 : 1;
  return std::make_pair(t * C * q.end()[-2], -t * C * p.end()[-2]);
}

    # Return (x, y) such that Ax+By=C.
# Assume that such (x, y) exists.
def dio(A, B, C):
    p, q = convergents(fraction(A, B))
    C //= A // p[-1]  # divide by gcd(A, B)
    t = (-1) if len(p) % 2 else 1
    return t * C * q[-2], -t * C * p[-2]

    Diophantine Approximation

    An important application of continued fraction theory is Diophantine approximation theory. Diophantine approximation refers to approximating real numbers with rational numbers. Of course, due to the density of rational numbers, if there are no restrictions, we can obtain approximations with arbitrarily small errors. Therefore, restrictions need to be imposed on which rational numbers can be used, such as only allowing rational numbers with denominators less than some value. This section discusses the relationship between the best approximations under such restrictions and continued fractions.

    Approximating Real Numbers with Convergents

    First, using the error estimation for convergents, we immediately obtain the following result:

    Theorem (Dirichlet)

    For an irrational number 𝑥x, there exist infinitely many reduced fractions 𝑝𝑞pq such that

    ∣𝑥−𝑝𝑞∣<1𝑞2|x−pq|<1q2

    holds.

    Proof

    According to the error estimation for convergents, for the 𝑘k-th convergent 𝑥𝑘 =𝑝𝑘𝑞𝑘xk=pkqk of an irrational number 𝑥x, we have

    ∣𝑥−𝑝𝑘𝑞𝑘∣≤1𝑞2𝑘.|x−pkqk|≤1qk2.

    By examining the proof of the error formula, we know that the equality condition does not hold for any irrational number 𝑥x. Therefore, all its convergents satisfy the requirement.

    This theorem can also be seen as a corollary of Dirichlet's approximation theorem. This is almost the best possible result. The exponent 2 in the denominator on the right-hand side cannot be improved, but the constant can be made better. Hurwitz's theorem shows that the right-hand side can be reduced to 1√5𝑞215q2, and this is the best bound.

    Hurwitz's theorem

    For an irrational number 𝑥x, there exist infinitely many reduced fractions 𝑝𝑞pq such that

    ∣𝑥−𝑝𝑞∣<1√5𝑞2|x−pq|<15q2

    holds, and the √55 on the right-hand side cannot be replaced by a larger real number.

    Proof (Borel)

    In fact, Borel proved that among every three consecutive convergents of an irrational number 𝑥x, at least one satisfies the above condition. Since there are infinitely many convergents and they are all reduced fractions, the first part of Hurwitz's theorem must hold.

    Proof by contradiction. Suppose there exists an irrational number 𝑥x and its convergents 𝑥𝑘−1,𝑥𝑘,𝑥𝑘+1xk−1,xk,xk+1 such that

    ∣𝑥−𝑝𝑘−1𝑞𝑘−1∣≥1√5𝑞2𝑘−1, ∣𝑥−𝑝𝑘𝑞𝑘∣≥1√5𝑞2𝑘, ∣𝑥−𝑝𝑘+1𝑞𝑘+1∣≥1√5𝑞2𝑘+1|x−pk−1qk−1|≥15qk−12, |x−pkqk|≥15qk2, |x−pk+1qk+1|≥15qk+12

    hold. Since consecutive convergents are necessarily on both sides of 𝑥x, by the difference formula we have

    1𝑞𝑘−1𝑞𝑘=∣𝑝𝑘−1𝑞𝑘−1−𝑝𝑘𝑞𝑘∣=∣𝑥−𝑝𝑘−1𝑞𝑘−1∣+∣𝑥−𝑝𝑘𝑞𝑘∣≥1√5𝑞2𝑘−1+1√5𝑞2𝑘.1qk−1qk=|pk−1qk−1−pkqk|=|x−pk−1qk−1|+|x−pkqk|≥15qk−12+15qk2.

    It can be rewritten as an inequality in terms of the ratio 𝑞𝑘𝑞𝑘−1qkqk−1

    𝑞𝑘𝑞𝑘−1+𝑞𝑘−1𝑞𝑘≤√5.qkqk−1+qk−1qk≤5.

    Since the left side is a rational number and the right side is an irrational number, the equality cannot hold. And since 𝑞𝑘 ≥𝑞𝑘−1qk≥qk−1, we can solve to get

    1≤𝑞𝑘𝑞𝑘−1<√5+12.1≤qkqk−1<5+12.

    Similarly, we can prove

    1≤𝑞𝑘+1𝑞𝑘<√5+12.1≤qk+1qk<5+12.

    However, according to the recurrence formula, combining the two equations, we have

    𝑎𝑘+1=𝑞𝑘+1𝑞𝑘−𝑞𝑘−1𝑞𝑘<√5+12−√5−12=1ak+1=qk+1qk−qk−1qk<5+12−5−12=1

    which contradicts the definition of simple continued fractions. Therefore, Borel's conclusion holds.

    To show that this bound is the best, we only need to find an 𝑥x such that for any 𝐶 >√5C>5, there are only finitely many reduced fractions 𝑝𝑞pq satisfying

    ∣𝑥−𝑝𝑞∣<1𝐶𝑞2|x−pq|<1Cq2

    holds. Below we prove that 𝜙 =√5+12ϕ=5+12 is such an 𝑥x.4

    Let 𝜙′ =−√5+12ϕ′=−5+12 be the conjugate root of 𝜙ϕ. They are both roots of the equation 𝑥2 −𝑥 −1 =0x2−x−1=0. Therefore, for any real number 𝑥x, we have

    𝑥2−𝑥−1=(𝑥−𝜙)(𝑥−𝜙′).x2−x−1=(x−ϕ)(x−ϕ′).

    Substituting the reduced fraction 𝑝𝑞pq, we obtain

    1𝑞2≤|𝑝2−𝑝𝑞−𝑞2|𝑞2=∣𝑝𝑞−𝜙∣∣𝑝𝑞−𝜙′∣≤∣𝑝𝑞−𝜙∣(∣𝑝𝑞−𝜙∣+|𝜙−𝜙′|)<1𝐶𝑞2(1𝐶𝑞2+𝑠𝑞𝑟𝑡5).1q2≤|p2−pq−q2|q2=|pq−ϕ||pq−ϕ′|≤|pq−ϕ|(|pq−ϕ|+|ϕ−ϕ′|)<1Cq2(1Cq2+sqrt5).

    For 𝐶 >√5C>5, we can directly solve to get 𝑞 <√𝐶(𝐶−√5)q<C(C−5), so it is impossible to have infinitely many solutions satisfying the above inequality.

    The proofs of these theorems show that convergents provide quite good Diophantine approximations. However, these may not be the best approximations. To discuss best approximations, we need to explain the measure of approximation quality. There are often two choices.

    Cases where the best approximation conclusions may not hold

    The next two sections will describe some results about best approximations. These results may not hold for some uninteresting cases. For example, both definitions of best approximations require strict inequality, but for a half-integer 𝑥 =𝑛 +12x=n+12 where 𝑛 ∈𝐙n∈Z, its continued fraction can be [𝑛,1,1][n,1,1]. At this time, its first two convergents 𝑥0 =𝑛x0=n and 𝑥1 =𝑛 +1x1=n+1 both have denominator 11, and their distances to 𝑥x are the same. This shows that neither is a best approximation. For the statements of conclusions in this section, readers should assume such cases are excluded. If readers do not care about the last few convergents, or only care about approximations of irrational numbers, then they do not need to worry about these extra complications.

    Best Approximations of the First Kind: Intermediate Fractions

    Best approximations of the first kind use

    ∣𝑥−𝑝𝑞∣|x−pq|

    to measure the quality of approximation.

    Best approximation of the first kind

    For a real number 𝑥x and a rational number 𝑝𝑞pq, if for any 𝑝′𝑞′ ≠𝑝𝑞p′q′≠pq with 0 <𝑞′ ≤𝑞0<q′≤q, we have

    ∣𝑥−𝑝𝑞∣<∣𝑥−𝑝′𝑞′∣,|x−pq|<|x−p′q′|,

    then 𝑝𝑞pq is called a best approximation of the first kind of 𝑥x.

    Best approximations of the first kind are not necessarily convergents, but a broader class of fractions.

    Intermediate fraction

    Let 𝑥x have convergents 𝑥𝑘+1 =[𝑎0,𝑎1,⋯,𝑎𝑘,𝑎𝑘+1]xk+1=[a0,a1,⋯,ak,ak+1], and let the integer 𝑡t satisfy 0 ≤𝑡 ≤𝑎𝑘+10≤t≤ak+15, then the fraction 𝑥𝑘,𝑡 =[𝑎0,𝑎1,⋯,𝑎𝑘,𝑡]xk,t=[a0,a1,⋯,ak,t] is called an intermediate fraction, semiconvergent, or secondary convergent of 𝑥x.6

    Similar to the case of convergents, intermediate fractions greater than (less than) 𝑥x are called upper (lower) semiconvergents.

    According to the recurrence formula, intermediate fractions can be written as

    𝑥𝑘,𝑡=𝑡𝑝𝑘+𝑝𝑘−1𝑡𝑞𝑘+𝑞𝑘−1.xk,t=tpk+pk−1tqk+qk−1.

    It must be a reduced fraction and lies between the convergents 𝑥𝑘−1xk−1 and 𝑥𝑘+1xk+1. As 𝑡t increases, it gradually approaches 𝑥𝑘+1xk+1: (taking the case where 𝑘k is even as an example)

    𝑥𝑘−1=𝑥𝑘,0<𝑥𝑘,1<𝑥𝑘,2<⋯<𝑥𝑘,𝑎𝑘+1=𝑥𝑘+1.xk−1=xk,0<xk,1<xk,2<⋯<xk,ak+1=xk+1.

    Because the numerators and denominators of convergents are both increasing, the numerators and denominators of intermediate fractions 𝑥𝑘,𝑡xk,t (𝑡 ≠0t≠0) lie between those of 𝑥𝑘xk and 𝑥𝑘+1xk+1. If these fractions are arranged by denominator size, intermediate fractions are some fractions between consecutive convergents.

    All best approximations of the first kind are intermediate fractions, but not all intermediate fractions are best approximations of the first kind.

    Theorem

    All best approximations of the first kind are intermediate fractions.

    Proof

    Because 𝑎0 ≤𝑥 ≤𝑎0 +1a0≤x≤a0+1, best approximations of the first kind must lie between 𝑥1,0 =𝑎0x1,0=a0 and 𝑥0,1 =𝑎0 +1x0,1=a0+1. All intermediate fractions in increasing order can be arranged as

    𝑥1,0<𝑥1,1<⋯<𝑥1,𝑎2=𝑥3,0<…<𝑥<…<𝑥2,0=𝑥0,𝑎1<⋯<𝑥0,1.x1,0<x1,1<⋯<x1,a2=x3,0<…<x<…<x2,0=x0,a1<⋯<x0,1.

    Intermediate fractions of the same order appear consecutively, and there are no gaps between intermediate fractions of different orders. This means that any rational number 𝑝𝑞pq lying between 𝑥1,0 =𝑎0x1,0=a0 and 𝑥0,1 =𝑎0 +1x0,1=a0+1 must lie between two intermediate fractions 𝑥𝑘,𝑡xk,t and 𝑥𝑘,𝑡+1xk,t+1 of the same order. Suppose it is not an intermediate fraction and is less than 𝑥x, then

    𝑥𝑘,𝑡<𝑝𝑞<𝑥𝑘,𝑡+1<𝑥.xk,t<pq<xk,t+1<x.

    On one hand, we have

    ∣𝑥𝑘,𝑡−𝑝𝑞∣≤|𝑥𝑘,𝑡−𝑥𝑘,𝑡+1|=1((𝑡+1)𝑞𝑘+𝑞𝑘−1)(𝑡𝑞𝑘+𝑞𝑘−1).|xk,t−pq|≤|xk,t−xk,t+1|=1((t+1)qk+qk−1)(tqk+qk−1).

    On the other hand, we have

    ∣𝑥𝑘,𝑡−𝑝𝑞∣=|𝑞(𝑡𝑝𝑘+𝑝𝑘−1)−𝑝((𝑡+1)𝑞𝑘+𝑞𝑘−1)|𝑞(𝑡𝑞𝑘+𝑞𝑘−1)≥1𝑞(𝑡𝑞𝑘+𝑞𝑘−1).|xk,t−pq|=|q(tpk+pk−1)−p((t+1)qk+qk−1)|q(tqk+qk−1)≥1q(tqk+qk−1).

    Therefore, we must have

    𝑞>(𝑡+1)𝑞𝑘+𝑞𝑘−1.q>(t+1)qk+qk−1.

    That is, the denominator of the rational number 𝑝𝑞pq is necessarily larger than that of 𝑥𝑘,𝑡+1xk,t+1, but it is not a better approximation:

    ∣𝑥−𝑝𝑞∣>|𝑥−𝑥𝑘,𝑡+1||x−pq|>|x−xk,t+1|

    Therefore, it cannot be a best approximation of the first kind. This shows that if it is not an intermediate fraction, it is not a best approximation of the first kind; that is, all best approximations of the first kind are intermediate fractions.

    Conversely, not all intermediate fractions can be asserted to be best approximations of the first kind. However, we can indeed give conditions for intermediate fractions to be best approximations of the first kind.

    Theorem

    All convergents are best approximations of the first kind. In addition, let 0 <𝑡 <𝑎𝑘+10<t<ak+1, then the intermediate fraction 𝑥𝑘,𝑡xk,t is a best approximation of the first kind if and only if 𝑡 >𝑎𝑘+12t>ak+12 or 𝑡 =𝑎𝑘+12t=ak+12 and 𝑟𝑘+2 >𝑞𝑘𝑞𝑘−1rk+2>qkqk−1.

    Proof

    Below we will prove that convergents are all best approximations of the second kind, so they are necessarily best approximations of the first kind. The key is on those intermediate fractions that are not convergents.

    As mentioned earlier, the denominator of the intermediate fraction 𝑥𝑘,𝑡xk,t lies between 𝑥𝑘xk and 𝑥𝑘+1xk+1, and as 𝑡t increases, it increases, but 𝑥𝑘,𝑡xk,t gets closer to 𝑥𝑘+1xk+1, thus getting closer to 𝑥x. Taking 𝑥𝑘,𝑡 <𝑥xk,t<x as an example, its relative position with neighboring intermediate fractions satisfies:

    𝑥𝑘−1<𝑥𝑘,𝑡<𝑥𝑘+1<𝑥<𝑥𝑘.xk−1<xk,t<xk+1<x<xk.

    Because the denominator of 𝑥𝑘xk is smaller than that of 𝑥𝑘,𝑡xk,t, the necessary condition for 𝑥𝑘,𝑡xk,t to be a best approximation of the first kind is that it is closer to 𝑥x than 𝑥𝑘xk. This is also sufficient because, as a convergent, there is no closer one with a smaller denominator, and those intermediate fractions with larger denominators than 𝑥𝑘xk must be of the same order as 𝑥𝑘,𝑡xk,t, but with smaller denominators, they must be farther from 𝑥x. For the errors of convergents and intermediate fractions, after calculation we have

    |𝑥𝑘−𝑥|=1𝑞𝑘(𝑟𝑘+1𝑞𝑘+𝑞𝑘−1),|𝑥𝑘,𝑡−𝑥|=∣𝑡𝑝𝑘+𝑝𝑘−1𝑡𝑞𝑘+𝑞𝑘−1−𝑟𝑘+1𝑝𝑘+𝑝𝑘−1𝑟𝑘+1𝑞𝑘+𝑞𝑘−1∣=𝑟𝑘+1−𝑡(𝑡𝑞𝑘+𝑞𝑘−1)(𝑟𝑘+1𝑞𝑘+𝑞𝑘−1).|xk−x|=1qk(rk+1qk+qk−1),|xk,t−x|=|tpk+pk−1tqk+qk−1−rk+1pk+pk−1rk+1qk+qk−1|=rk+1−t(tqk+qk−1)(rk+1qk+qk−1).

    Here we used 𝑟𝑘+1 ≥𝑎𝑘+1 >𝑡rk+1≥ak+1>t. Therefore, 𝑥𝑘,𝑡xk,t is closer to 𝑥x than 𝑥𝑘xk, becoming a best approximation of the first kind, if and only if

    𝑟𝑘+1−𝑡𝑡𝑞𝑘+𝑞𝑘−1<1𝑞𝑘⟺𝑟𝑘+1<2𝑡+𝑞𝑘−1𝑞𝑘.rk+1−ttqk+qk−1<1qk⟺rk+1<2t+qk−1qk.

    At this time, there are three possible situations:

    1. If 𝑡 <𝑎𝑘+12t<ak+12, then 2𝑡 <𝑎𝑘+12t<ak+1. Since both sides are integers, 2𝑡 ≤𝑎𝑘+1 −12t≤ak+1−1, so 2𝑡 +𝑞𝑘−1𝑞𝑘 ≤2𝑡 +1 ≤𝑎𝑘+1 ≤𝑟𝑘+12t+qk−1qk≤2t+1≤ak+1≤rk+1. At this time, 𝑥𝑘,𝑡xk,t is not a best approximation of the first kind;
    2. If 𝑡 >𝑎𝑘+12t>ak+12, then 2𝑡 >𝑎𝑘+12t>ak+1. Since both sides are integers, 2𝑡 ≥𝑎𝑘+1 +1 >𝑟𝑘+12t≥ak+1+1>rk+1. At this time, 𝑥𝑘,𝑡xk,t is a best approximation of the first kind;
    3. If 𝑎𝑘+1ak+1 is even, there is a third case, i.e., 𝑡 =𝑎𝑘+12t=ak+12. The above condition is equivalent to 1𝑟𝑘+1 =𝑟𝑘+1 −𝑎𝑘+1 <𝑞𝑘−1𝑞𝑘1rk+1=rk+1−ak+1<qk−1qk, that is, 𝑟𝑘+2 >𝑞𝑘𝑞𝑘−1rk+2>qkqk−1.

    Therefore, if all best approximations of the first kind of a real number 𝑥x are arranged in increasing order by denominator, they will be divided into several segments according to their relationship with 𝑥x. Each segment consists of some (possibly zero) consecutive intermediate fractions of the same order, and always ends with a convergent. Within each segment, it stays on one side of the real number 𝑥x, and segments alternate on both sides of 𝑥x.

    𝜋 =[3,7,15,1,292,⋯]π=[3,7,15,1,292,⋯], so the first 15 best approximations of the first kind with smallest denominators are:

    𝑥0=31, 𝑥0,4=134, 𝑥0,5=165, 𝑥0,6=196, 𝑥1=227,𝑥1,8=17957, 𝑥1,9=20164, 𝑥1,10=22371, 𝑥1,11=24578, 𝑥1,12=26785,𝑥1,13=28992, 𝑥1,14=31199, 𝑥2=333106, 𝑥3=355113, 𝑥3,146=5216316604.x0=31, x0,4=134, x0,5=165, x0,6=196, x1=227,x1,8=17957, x1,9=20164, x1,10=22371, x1,11=24578, x1,12=26785,x1,13=28992, x1,14=31199, x2=333106, x3=355113, x3,146=5216316604.

    Best Approximations of the Second Kind

    Best approximations of the second kind use |𝑞𝑥 −𝑝||qx−p| to measure the quality of approximation.

    Best approximation of the second kind

    For a real number 𝑥x and a rational number 𝑝𝑞pq, if for any 𝑝′𝑞′ ≠𝑝𝑞p′q′≠pq with 0 <𝑞′ ≤𝑞0<q′≤q, we have

    |𝑞𝑥−𝑝|<|𝑞′𝑥−𝑝′|,|qx−p|<|q′x−p′|,

    then 𝑝𝑞pq is called a best approximation of the second kind of 𝑥x.

    The condition for best approximations of the second kind is equivalent to

    ∣𝑥−𝑝𝑞∣<𝑞′𝑞∣𝑥−𝑝′𝑞′∣.|x−pq|<q′q|x−p′q′|.

    Since 𝑞′ ≤𝑞q′≤q, the condition for best approximations of the second kind is more stringent than that for best approximations of the first kind.

    Best approximations of the second kind can and only can be convergents.

    Theorem

    All best approximations of the second kind must be convergents, and all convergents must be best approximations of the second kind.

    Proof

    To prove the first part, since best approximations of the second kind must also be best approximations of the first kind, we only need to prove that intermediate fractions that are not convergents cannot be best approximations of the second kind. To do this, let 𝑥𝑘,𝑡 =𝑝𝑞xk,t=pq be an intermediate fraction but not a convergent, and suppose 𝑥𝑘,𝑡 <𝑥xk,t<x, then

    𝑥𝑘−1<𝑥𝑘,𝑡<𝑥𝑘+1<𝑥<𝑥𝑘.xk−1<xk,t<xk+1<x<xk.

    Since the error between 𝑥𝑘,𝑡xk,t and 𝑥x

    |𝑥𝑘,𝑡−𝑥|≥|𝑥𝑘,𝑡−𝑥𝑘+1|=∣𝑝𝑞−𝑝𝑘+1𝑞𝑘+1∣=|𝑝𝑞𝑘+1−𝑝𝑘+1𝑞|𝑞𝑞𝑘+1≥1𝑞𝑞𝑘+1,|xk,t−x|≥|xk,t−xk+1|=|pq−pk+1qk+1|=|pqk+1−pk+1q|qqk+1≥1qqk+1,

    and using the error estimation for convergents, we always have

    |𝑞𝑥𝑘,𝑡−𝑝|≥1𝑞𝑘+1≥|𝑞𝑘𝑥𝑘−𝑝𝑘|,|qxk,t−p|≥1qk+1≥|qkxk−pk|,

    so the approximation quality of 𝑥𝑘,𝑡xk,t is no better than that of 𝑥𝑘xk with a smaller denominator, so it cannot be a best approximation of the second kind.

    Conversely, to prove the second part, i.e., that every convergent 𝑥𝑘 =𝑝𝑘𝑞𝑘xk=pkqk is a best approximation of the second kind. This means that for all fractions 𝑝𝑞pq with 𝑞 ≤𝑞𝑘q≤qk, we have |𝑞𝑘𝑥 −𝑝𝑘| <|𝑞𝑥 −𝑝||qkx−pk|<|qx−p|. Without considering half-integers, we can assume 𝑘 >0k>0. First, according to the error estimation for convergents approximating real numbers,

    |𝑞𝑘−1𝑥−𝑝𝑘−1|≥1𝑞𝑘−1+𝑞𝑘≥1𝑞𝑘+1≥|𝑞𝑘𝑥−𝑝𝑘|.|qk−1x−pk−1|≥1qk−1+qk≥1qk+1≥|qkx−pk|.

    All inequalities hold with equality if and only if 𝑎𝑘+1 =1ak+1=1 and it is the last term of the continued fraction. Without considering such cases, then 𝑥𝑘−1 =𝑝𝑘−1𝑞𝑘−1xk−1=pk−1qk−1 is strictly worse than 𝑥𝑘 =𝑝𝑘𝑞𝑘xk=pkqk.

    Take any fraction 𝑝𝑞 ≠𝑥𝑘pq≠xk with 0 <𝑞 ≤𝑞𝑘0<q≤qk. Since we have the difference formula 𝑝𝑘𝑞𝑘−1 −𝑝𝑘−1𝑞𝑘 =( −1)𝑘−1pkqk−1−pk−1qk=(−1)k−1, by Cramer's rule, the system of linear equations

    {𝜆𝑝𝑘+𝜇𝑝𝑘−1=𝑝,𝜆𝑞𝑘+𝜇𝑞𝑘−1=𝑞{λpk+μpk−1=p,λqk+μqk−1=q

    must have a unique integer solution (𝜆,𝜇)(λ,μ). If 𝜆𝜇 >0λμ>0, then 𝑞 >|𝜆|𝑞𝑘 ≥𝑞𝑘q>|λ|qk≥qk, a contradiction. Otherwise, 𝜆𝜇 ≤0λμ≤0, i.e., 𝜆λ and 𝜇μ have opposite signs. Then since 𝑞𝑘−1𝑥 −𝑝𝑘−1qk−1x−pk−1 and 𝑞𝑘𝑥 −𝑝𝑘qkx−pk also have opposite signs, we have 𝜆(𝑞𝑘−1𝑥 −𝑝𝑘−1)λ(qk−1x−pk−1) and 𝜇(𝑞𝑘𝑥 −𝑝𝑘)μ(qkx−pk) having the same sign, so

    |𝑞𝑥−𝑝|=|𝜆||𝑞𝑘𝑥−𝑝𝑘|+|𝜇||𝑞𝑘−1𝑥−𝑝𝑘−1|>|𝑞𝑘𝑥−𝑝𝑘|.|qx−p|=|λ||qkx−pk|+|μ||qk−1x−pk−1|>|qkx−pk|.

    The last inequality is strict because 𝑥𝑘−1xk−1 is strictly worse than 𝑥𝑘xk, and 𝑝𝑞 ≠𝑥𝑘pq≠xk. This shows that 𝑥𝑘xk is a best approximation of the second kind.

    This property shows that convergents are indeed quite good Diophantine approximations.

    Determining Convergents

    Best approximations of the second kind provide necessary and sufficient conditions for determining whether a fraction is a convergent. This shows that we can judge whether a fraction is a convergent by checking the relative quality of its approximation. Legendre's criterion provides a method to judge convergents based on the absolute quality of approximation. The original statement of Legendre's criterion provides necessary and sufficient conditions, but its form is not practical. This section provides a simplified version of Legendre's criterion and shows that it does not miss too many convergents.

    Theorem (Legendre)

    For a real number 𝑥x and a fraction 𝑝𝑞pq, if

    ∣𝑥−𝑝𝑞∣<12𝑞2|x−pq|<12q2

    then 𝑝𝑞pq must be a convergent of 𝑥x.

    Proof

    Let 𝜖 ∈{ −1,1}ϵ∈{−1,1} and 𝜃 ∈(0,1/2)θ∈(0,1/2) be the constants such that

    𝑥−𝑝𝑞=𝜖𝜃𝑞2x−pq=ϵθq2

    holds. Expand the rational number 𝑝𝑞pq into the continued fraction [𝑎0,𝑎1,⋯,𝑎𝑛][a0,a1,⋯,an]. Here, a rational number has two continued fraction representations, and their 𝑛n differs by exactly one, so we can choose the continued fraction representation such that ( −1)𝑛 =𝜖(−1)n=ϵ, and denote the convergent of this continued fraction representation as 𝑝𝑘𝑞𝑘pkqk. Let 𝜔ω satisfy

    𝑥=𝜔𝑝𝑛+𝑝𝑛−1𝜔𝑞𝑛+𝑞𝑛−1.x=ωpn+pn−1ωqn+qn−1.

    Then we must have

    𝜖𝜃𝑞2=𝑥−𝑝𝑞=𝑥−𝑝𝑛𝑞𝑛=𝑝𝑛−1𝑞𝑛−𝑝𝑛𝑞𝑛−1(𝜔𝑞𝑛+𝑞𝑛−1)𝑞𝑛=(−1)𝑛(𝜔𝑞𝑛+𝑞𝑛−1)𝑞𝑛.ϵθq2=x−pq=x−pnqn=pn−1qn−pnqn−1(ωqn+qn−1)qn=(−1)n(ωqn+qn−1)qn.

    Hence, we have

    𝜃=𝑞𝑛𝜔𝑞𝑛+𝑞𝑛−1.θ=qnωqn+qn−1.

    This shows that

    𝜔=1𝜃−𝑞𝑛−1𝑞𝑛>1.ω=1θ−qn−1qn>1.

    Expand 𝜔ω into the continued fraction [𝑏0,𝑏1,⋯][b0,b1,⋯], then

    𝑥=𝜔𝑝𝑛+𝑝𝑛−1𝜔𝑞𝑛+𝑞𝑛−1=[𝑎0,𝑎1,⋯,𝑎𝑛,𝜔]=[𝑎0,𝑎1,⋯,𝑎𝑛,𝑏0,𝑏1,⋯].x=ωpn+pn−1ωqn+qn−1=[a0,a1,⋯,an,ω]=[a0,a1,⋯,an,b0,b1,⋯].

    This is a valid simple continued fraction, so 𝑝𝑞pq is a convergent of 𝑥x.

    This proof actually shows that the necessary and sufficient condition for 𝑝𝑞pq to be a convergent is that 𝜔 >1ω>1 in the above proof, which is the original form of Legendre's criterion.

    This criterion shows that as long as the quality of approximation is good enough, it must be a convergent. The next theorem shows that there are enough such good convergents: at least half of all convergents satisfy this condition.

    Theorem (Valhen)

    Among every two consecutive convergents of a real number 𝑥x, at least one satisfies

    ∣𝑥−𝑝𝑞∣<12𝑞2.|x−pq|<12q2.
    Proof

    Suppose not. There exists a real number 𝑥x with two consecutive convergents 𝑥𝑘−1xk−1 and 𝑥𝑘xk satisfying

    ∣𝑥−𝑝𝑘𝑞𝑘∣≥12𝑞2𝑘, ∣𝑥−𝑝𝑘+1𝑞𝑘+1∣≥12𝑞2𝑘+1.|x−pkqk|≥12qk2, |x−pk+1qk+1|≥12qk+12.

    Since 𝑥x lies between 𝑥𝑘−1xk−1 and 𝑥𝑘xk,

    12𝑞2𝑘+12𝑞2𝑘+1≤∣𝑥−𝑝𝑘𝑞𝑘∣+∣𝑥−𝑝𝑘+1𝑞𝑘+1∣=∣𝑝𝑘𝑞𝑘−𝑝𝑘+1𝑞𝑘+1∣=1𝑞𝑘𝑞𝑘+1.12qk2+12qk+12≤|x−pkqk|+|x−pk+1qk+1|=|pkqk−pk+1qk+1|=1qkqk+1.

    This shows 𝑞𝑘 =𝑞𝑘+1qk=qk+1. Therefore, we must have 𝑘 =0k=0 and 𝑎1 =1a1=1. At this time, the first two convergents are 𝑥0 =𝑎0x0=a0 and 𝑥1 =𝑎0 +1x1=a0+1. So the only counterexample is a half-integer, which according to the earlier explanation, is not considered in this article.

    Geometric Interpretation

    Continued fraction theory has an elegant geometric interpretation.

    As shown in the figure, for a real number 𝜉 >0ξ>0, the line 𝑦 =𝜉𝑥y=ξx divides the lattice points in the first quadrant (including points on the 𝑥x and 𝑦y axes but excluding the origin, the same applies below) into upper and lower parts. For rational numbers 𝜉ξ, points on the line 𝑦 =𝜉𝑥y=ξx count as both upper and lower points. Consider the convex hulls of these two sets of points. Then odd-indexed convergents are vertices of the convex hull of the upper part, and even-indexed convergents are vertices of the convex hull of the lower part. Lattice points on the line segment between two adjacent vertices of the convex hull are intermediate fractions. The figure shows the convergents and intermediate fractions (gray points) for 𝜉 =97ξ=97.

    Most conclusions about continued fractions in the earlier sections have corresponding geometric interpretations:

    Geometric interpretation
    • Each fraction 𝜈 =𝑝𝑞ν=pq corresponds to a lattice point ⃗𝜈 =(𝑞,𝑝)ν→=(q,p) in the first quadrant, and the size of the fraction corresponds to the slope of the line connecting it with the origin.

    • The direction vector of the line 𝑦 =𝜉𝑥y=ξx is ⃗𝜉 =(1,𝜉)ξ→=(1,ξ). Using the concept of cross product (𝑥1,𝑦1) ×(𝑥2,𝑦2) =𝑥1𝑦2 −𝑥2𝑦1(x1,y1)×(x2,y2)=x1y2−x2y1, we can determine whether a point is above or below the line by the sign of ⃗𝜉 ×⃗𝜈 =𝑝 −𝑞𝜉ξ→×ν→=p−qξ. Therefore, points above the line correspond to fractions greater than or equal to 𝜉ξ, and points below the line correspond to fractions less than or equal to 𝜉ξ. The absolute value |⃗𝜉 ×⃗𝜈||ξ→×ν→| is proportional to the distance from the point ⃗𝜈ν→ to the line 𝑦 =𝑥𝑖𝑥y=xix

      |𝑝−𝑞𝑥|√1+𝜉2,|p−qx|1+ξ2,

      which corresponds to the quality of approximation of the fraction 𝜈ν to the real number 𝜉ξ.

    • Let the point corresponding to the convergent 𝜉𝑘 =𝑝𝑘𝑞𝑘ξk=pkqk be ⃗𝜉𝑘 =(𝑝𝑘,𝑞𝑘)ξ→k=(pk,qk), then the recurrence formula can be written as

      ⃗𝜉𝑘=𝑎𝑘⃗𝜉𝑘−1+⃗𝜉𝑘−2.ξ→k=akξ→k−1+ξ→k−2.

      The starting points of the recurrence are 𝜉−2 =(1,0)ξ−2=(1,0) and 𝜉−1 =(0,1)ξ−1=(0,1).

    • For an integer 𝑡t, if 0 ≤𝑡 ≤𝑎𝑘0≤t≤ak, then the point

      ⃗𝜉𝑘−1,𝑡=𝑡⃗𝜉𝑘−1+⃗𝜉𝑘−2ξ→k−1,t=tξ→k−1+ξ→k−2

      lies on the line segment connecting ⃗𝜉𝑘−2ξ→k−2 and ⃗𝜉𝑘ξ→k. They correspond to the intermediate fraction 𝜉𝑘−1,𝑡ξk−1,t.

    • Using geometric methods, we can construct all convergents and intermediate fractions. Starting from the points ⃗𝜉−2 =(1,0)ξ→−2=(1,0) and ⃗𝜉−1 =(0,1)ξ→−1=(0,1), these two points are on opposite sides of the line 𝑦 =𝜉𝑥y=ξx, which means ⃗𝜉 ×⃗𝜉−2ξ→×ξ→−2 and ⃗𝜉 ×⃗𝜉−1ξ→×ξ→−1 have opposite signs. Add ⃗𝜉−1ξ→−1 to ⃗𝜉−2ξ→−2 by vector addition until we cannot continue without crossing the line 𝑦 =𝑥𝑖𝑥y=xix, and denote the result as ⃗𝜉0ξ→0. At this time, it is still on a different side from ⃗𝜉−1ξ→−1. Then add ⃗𝜉0ξ→0 to ⃗𝜉−1ξ→−1 until we cannot continue without crossing the line 𝑦 =𝑥𝑖𝑥y=xix, and denote the result as ⃗𝜉1ξ→1. At this time, it is still on a different side from ⃗𝜉0ξ→0. This process can continue indefinitely, unless at some finite step a ⃗𝜉𝑛ξ→n exactly lies on the line 𝑦 =𝑥𝑖𝑥y=xix. The latter means the vectors ⃗𝜉ξ→ and ⃗𝜉𝑛ξ→n are collinear, i.e., 𝜉 =𝑝𝑛𝑞𝑛ξ=pnqn is rational. This process produces the shapes shown in the earlier diagrams. Boris Delaunay vividly called this process the nose-stretching algorithm9.

    • If we need to quickly calculate how many times to add ⃗𝜉𝑘−1ξ→k−1 to ⃗𝜉𝑘−2ξ→k−2 at each step, we can use the cross product. Because ⃗𝜉 ×⃗𝜉𝑘−1ξ→×ξ→k−1 and ⃗𝜉 ×⃗𝜉𝑘−2ξ→×ξ→k−2 have opposite signs, if we denote ⃗𝜉𝑘−1,𝑡 =𝑡⃗𝜉𝑘−1 +⃗𝜉𝑘−2ξ→k−1,t=tξ→k−1+ξ→k−2 as the result of adding ⃗𝜉𝑘−1ξ→k−1 to ⃗𝜉𝑘−2ξ→k−2 𝑡t times, then ⃗𝜉 ×⃗𝜉𝑘−1,𝑡 =𝑡(⃗𝜉 ×⃗𝜉𝑘−1) +(⃗𝜉 ×⃗𝜉𝑘−2)ξ→×ξ→k−1,t=t(ξ→×ξ→k−1)+(ξ→×ξ→k−2) not changing sign means we have not crossed the line. Before the sign changes, the absolute value of ⃗𝜉 ×⃗𝜉𝑘−1,𝑡ξ→×ξ→k−1,t gradually decreases. Denote

      𝑟𝑘=∣⃗𝜉×⃗𝜉𝑘−2⃗𝜉×⃗𝜉𝑘−1∣=−⃗𝜉×⃗𝜉𝑘−2⃗𝜉×⃗𝜉𝑘−1.rk=|ξ→×ξ→k−2ξ→×ξ→k−1|=−ξ→×ξ→k−2ξ→×ξ→k−1.

      Then the maximum number of times it can decrease is

      𝑎𝑘=⌊𝑟𝑘⌋=⌊∣𝑞𝑘−1𝜉−𝑝𝑘−1𝑞𝑘−2𝜉−𝑝𝑘−2∣⌋.ak=⌊rk⌋=⌊|qk−1ξ−pk−1qk−2ξ−pk−2|⌋.

      This is the 𝑘k-th term of the continued fraction expansion. Moreover, 𝑟𝑘rk is the remainder of the continued fraction expansion, which satisfies:

      𝑟𝑘=−𝑞𝑘−1𝜉−𝑝𝑘−1𝑞𝑘−2𝜉−𝑝𝑘−2⟺𝜉=𝑝𝑘−1𝑟𝑘+𝑝𝑘−2𝑞𝑘−1𝑟𝑘+𝑞𝑘−2.rk=−qk−1ξ−pk−1qk−2ξ−pk−2⟺ξ=pk−1rk+pk−2qk−1rk+qk−2.

      This is the continued fraction relation 𝜉 =[𝑎0,𝑎1,⋯,𝑎𝑘−1,𝑟𝑘]ξ=[a0,a1,⋯,ak−1,rk].

    • Because the change in ⃗𝜉 ×⃗𝜉𝑘−1,𝑡ξ→×ξ→k−1,t caused by each addition of vectors has step size |⃗𝜉 ×⃗𝜉𝑘−1||ξ→×ξ→k−1|, the final remaining distance |⃗𝜉 ×⃗𝜉𝑘||ξ→×ξ→k| must be strictly less than |⃗𝜉 ×⃗𝜉𝑘−1||ξ→×ξ→k−1|. This shows that the approximation quality of convergents (measured by |𝑞𝑥 −𝑝||qx−p|) strictly improves as 𝑘k increases.

    • Using the properties of cross products, we have

      ⃗𝜉𝑘×⃗𝜉𝑘+1=⃗𝜉𝑘×(𝑎𝑘+1⃗𝜉𝑘+⃗𝜉𝑘−1)=⃗𝜉𝑘×⃗𝜉𝑘−1=−⃗𝜉𝑘−1×⃗𝜉𝑘.ξ→k×ξ→k+1=ξ→k×(ak+1ξ→k+ξ→k−1)=ξ→k×ξ→k−1=−ξ→k−1×ξ→k.

      By induction, we have

      ⃗𝜉𝑘×⃗𝜉𝑘+1=(−1)𝑘+2⃗𝜉𝑘−2×⃗𝜉𝑘−1=(−1)𝑘.ξ→k×ξ→k+1=(−1)k+2ξ→k−2×ξ→k−1=(−1)k.

      This is the difference formula for convergents 𝑝𝑘+1𝑞𝑘 −𝑝𝑘𝑞𝑘+1 =( −1)𝑘pk+1qk−pkqk+1=(−1)k.

    • The area between the two convex hulls can be divided into several (possibly infinitely many) triangles, where each triangle's vertices are ⃗𝜉𝑘−2ξ→k−2, ⃗𝜉𝑘ξ→k, and ⃗00→. The area of such a triangle is

      12|⃗𝜉𝑘−2×⃗𝜉𝑘|=12|⃗𝜉𝑘−2×(𝑎𝑘⃗𝜉𝑘−1+⃗𝜉𝑘−2)|=𝑎𝑘2|⃗𝜉𝑘−2×⃗𝜉𝑘−1|=𝑎𝑘2.12|ξ→k−2×ξ→k|=12|ξ→k−2×(akξ→k−1+ξ→k−2)|=ak2|ξ→k−2×ξ→k−1|=ak2.

      According to Pick's theorem, this means that if we let 𝐼I and 𝐵B be the numbers of interior and boundary lattice points of the triangle respectively, then

      𝐼+𝐵2−1=𝑎𝑘2.I+B2−1=ak2.

      It is known that there are already {⃗0} ∪{⃗𝜉𝑘−1,𝑡 :0 ≤𝑡 ≤𝑎𝑘}{0→}∪{ξ→k−1,t:0≤t≤ak} totaling 𝑎𝑘 +2ak+2 lattice points on the boundary. This shows that 𝐼 =0I=0 and 𝐵 =𝑎𝑘 +2B=ak+2. Therefore, there are no more lattice points on the edges of the triangle, and no interior lattice points either. That is, 𝑞𝑘qk and 𝑝𝑘pk are reduced, and intermediate fractions are all lattice points on the edge connecting ⃗𝜉𝑘−2ξ→k−2 and ⃗𝜉𝑘ξ→k, and all lattice points in the first quadrant are inside the two convex hulls.

    The two convex hulls obtained in this way are called the Klein polygon. Similar definitions can be made in higher-dimensional spaces, yielding the Klein polyhedron, which can extend the concept of continued fractions to higher-dimensional spaces.

    Continued Fraction Trees

    Main article: Stern–Brocot Tree and Farey Sequences

    The Stern–Brocot tree is a binary search tree storing all fractions in [0,∞][0,∞]. Finite continued fractions actually encode the path from the root of the Stern–Brocot tree to where a fraction is located. That is, the continued fraction representation of a rational number 𝑥x [𝑎0,𝑎1,⋯,𝑎𝑛−1,1][a0,a1,⋯,an−1,1] means that starting from the tree root 1111, we need to move to the right child node 𝑎0a0 times, then to the left child node 𝑎1a1 times, alternating directions, until we have moved 𝑎𝑛−1an−1 times in some direction. Note that only continued fraction representations ending with 11 can be used here.

    Understanding continued fraction representations as paths on the Stern–Brocot tree allows us to obtain algorithms for comparing continued fractions.

    Comparing continued fractions

    Given continued fractions 𝛼 =[𝛼0,𝛼1,⋯,𝛼𝑛]α=[α0,α1,⋯,αn] and 𝛽 =[𝛽0,𝛽1,⋯,𝛽𝑚]β=[β0,β1,⋯,βm], compare their sizes.

    Solution

    First, convert both continued fractions to the form ending with 11. Let the given continued fractions already be in this form, i.e., 𝛼𝑛 =𝛽𝑚 =1αn=βm=1. Since even positions (with indices starting from 00) are the number of moves to the right, and odd positions are the number of moves to the left, we have 𝛼 <𝛽α<β if and only if, when compared in lexicographic order,

    (𝛼0,−𝛼1,𝛼2,⋯,(−1)𝑛−1𝛼𝑛−1,0,⋯)<(𝛽0,−𝛽1,𝛽2,⋯,(−1)𝑚−1𝛽𝑚−1,0,⋯).(α0,−α1,α2,⋯,(−1)n−1αn−1,0,⋯)<(β0,−β1,β2,⋯,(−1)m−1βm−1,0,⋯).

    Compared to the continued fraction representation, we alternately add positive and negative signs, delete the trailing 11, and pad positions with insufficient length with 00.

    // Expand [..., n] to [..., n-1, 1] if needed.
void expand(std::vector<int>& a) {
  if (a.size() == 1 || a.back() > 1) {
    --a.back();
    a.push_back(1);
  }
}

// Check if a is smaller than b.
bool less_than(std::vector<int> a, std::vector<int> b) {
  expand(a);
  expand(b);
  for (int i = 0; i < a.size() - 1 || i < b.size() - 1; ++i) {
    int d = (i < a.size() - 1 ? a[i] : 0) - (i < b.size() - 1 ? b[i] : 0);
    if (i & 1) d = -d;
    if (d < 0) {
      return true;
    } else if (d > 0) {
      return false;
    }
  }
  return false;
}

    # Expand [..., n] to [..., n-1, 1] if needed.
def expand(a):
    if a[-1] != 1 or len(a) == 1:
        a[-1] -= 1
        a.append(1)
    return a


# Check if a is smaller than b.
def less_than(a, b):
    a = expand(a)
    b = expand(b)
    a = [(-1) ** i * a[i] for i in range(len(a))]
    b = [(-1) ** i * b[i] for i in range(len(b))]
    return a < b
    Best interior point

    For 01 ≤𝑝0𝑞0 <𝑝1𝑞1 ≤1001≤p0q0<p1q1≤10, find the rational number 𝑝𝑞pq satisfying 𝑝0𝑞0 <𝑝𝑞 <𝑝1𝑞1p0q0<pq<p1q1 with minimal (𝑞,𝑝)(q,p).

    Solution

    Since the Stern–Brocot tree is both a binary search tree for fractions in [0,∞][0,∞] and a Cartesian tree for pairs (𝑞,𝑝)(q,p), the problem can almost be transformed into finding the LCA (least common ancestor) of two points on the Stern–Brocot tree. However, LCA can only handle closed intervals, and the LCA may be one of the endpoints themselves. To avoid additional discussions, we can first construct 𝑝0𝑞0 +𝜀p0q0+ε and 𝑝1𝑞1 −𝜀p1q1−ε, then compute the LCA. After the path from the root to the node has been computed through continued fractions, the LCA is simply the longest common path.

    To construct 𝑥 ±𝜀x±ε, we only need to first move right (left) once at node 𝑥x, then move left (right) ∞∞ times. Converting to the language of continued fractions, for a fraction 𝑥 =[𝑎0,𝑎1,⋯,𝑎𝑛−1,1]x=[a0,a1,⋯,an−1,1], we know that 𝑥 ±𝜀x±ε must be [𝑎0,𝑎1,⋯,𝑎𝑛−1 +1,∞][a0,a1,⋯,an−1+1,∞] and [𝑎0,𝑎1,⋯,𝑎𝑛−1,1,∞][a0,a1,⋯,an−1,1,∞], so we only need to compare these two continued fractions, and define the larger (smaller) one as 𝑥 ±𝜀x±ε.

    // Get X +- EPSILON.
auto pm_eps(std::vector<int> a) {
  constexpr int inf = 0x3f3f3f3f;
  // Deal with empty continued fraction for 1/0.
  if (a.empty()) {
    a.emplace_back(inf);
  }
  auto b = a;
  expand(b);
  a.emplace_back(inf);
  b.emplace_back(inf);
  return less_than(a, b) ? std::make_pair(a, b) : std::make_pair(b, a);
}

// Find the lexicographically smallest (q, p)
//   such that p0/q0 < p/q < p1/q1.
auto middle(int p0, int q0, int p1, int q1) {
  auto a0 = pm_eps(fraction(p0, q0)).second;
  auto a1 = pm_eps(fraction(p1, q1)).first;
  std::vector<int> a;
  for (int i = 0; i < a0.size() || i < a1.size(); ++i) {
    if (a0[i] == a1[i]) {
      a.emplace_back(a0[i]);
    } else {
      a.emplace_back(std::min(a0[i], a1[i]) + 1);
      break;
    }
  }
  auto pq = convergents(a);
  return std::make_pair(pq.first.back(), pq.second.back());
}

    # Get X +- EPSILON.
def pm_eps(a):
    # Deal with empty continued fraction for 1/0.
    if not a:
        a.append(float("inf"))
    b = expand(a.copy())
    a.append(float("inf"))
    b.append(float("inf"))
    return (a, b) if less_than(a, b) else (b, a)


# Find the lexicographically smallest (q, p)
#   such that p0/q0 < p/q < p1/q1.
def middle(p0, q0, p1, q1):
    a0 = pm_eps(fraction(p0, q0))[1]
    a1 = pm_eps(fraction(p1, q1))[0]
    a = []
    for i in range(min(len(a0), len(a1))):
        if a0[i] == a1[i]:
            a.append(a0[i])
        else:
            a.append(int(min(a0[i], a1[i])) + 1)
            break
    p, q = convergents(a)
    return p[-1], q[-1]
    GCJ 2019, Round 2 - New Elements: Part 2

    Given 𝑁N pairs of positive integers (𝐶𝑖,𝐽𝑖)(Ci,Ji), find a pair of positive integers (𝑥,𝑦)(x,y) such that {𝐶𝑖𝑥 +𝐽𝑖𝑦}{Cix+Jiy} is strictly increasing. Among all pairs satisfying the requirements, output the lexicographically smallest pair.

    Solution

    Let 𝐴𝑖 =𝐶𝑖 −𝐶𝑖−1Ai=Ci−Ci−1 and 𝐵𝑖 =𝐽𝑖 −𝐽𝑖−1Bi=Ji−Ji−1. The problem transforms into finding (𝑥,𝑦)(x,y) such that all 𝐴𝑖𝑥 +𝐵𝑖𝑦Aix+Biy are integers. These pairs can be divided into four cases:

    1. The case 𝐴𝑖,𝐵𝑖 >0Ai,Bi>0 can be ignored because we already assume (𝑥,𝑦) >0(x,y)>0;
    2. The case 𝐴𝑖,𝐵𝑖 ≤0Ai,Bi≤0 directly outputs "IMPOSSIBLE";
    3. The case 𝐴𝑖 >0,𝐵𝑖 ≤0Ai>0,Bi≤0 is equivalent to the constraint 𝑦𝑥 <𝐴𝑖−𝐵𝑖yx<Ai−Bi;
    4. The case 𝐴𝑖 ≤0,𝐵𝑖 >0Ai≤0,Bi>0 is equivalent to the constraint 𝑦𝑥 >−𝐴𝑖𝐵𝑖yx>−AiBi.

    Therefore, take 𝑝0𝑞0p0q0 as the largest −𝐴𝑖𝐵𝑖−AiBi in the fourth case, and take 𝑝1𝑞1p1q1 as the smallest 𝐴𝑖−𝐵𝑖Ai−Bi in the third case. The original problem becomes finding (𝑞,𝑝)(q,p) in lexicographically smallest order such that 𝑝0𝑞0 <𝑝𝑞 <𝑝1𝑞1p0q0<pq<p1q1 holds.

    void solve() {
  int n;
  std::cin >> n;
  std::vector<int> C(n), J(n);
  // p0/q0 < y/x < p1/q1
  int p0 = 0, q0 = 1, p1 = 1, q1 = 0;
  bool fail = false;
  for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) {
    std::cin >> C[i] >> J[i];
    if (i) {
      int A = C[i] - C[i - 1];
      int B = J[i] - J[i - 1];
      if (A <= 0 && B <= 0) {
        fail = true;
        break;
      } else if (B > 0 && A < 0) {  // y/x > (-A)/B if B > 0
        if ((-A) * q0 > p0 * B) {
          p0 = -A;
          q0 = B;
        }
      } else if (B < 0 && A > 0) {  // y/x < A/(-B) if B < 0
        if (A * q1 < p1 * (-B)) {
          p1 = A;
          q1 = -B;
        }
      }
    }
  }
  if (fail || p0 * q1 >= p1 * q0) {
    printf("IMPOSSIBLE\n");
  } else {
    auto pq = middle(p0, q0, p1, q1);
    printf("%d %d\n", pq.first, pq.second);
  }
}

    def solve():
    n = int(input())
    C = [0] * n
    J = [0] * n
    # p0/q0 < y/x < p1/q1
    p0, q0 = 0, 1
    p1, q1 = 1, 0
    fail = False
    for i in range(n):
        C[i], J[i] = map(int, input().split())
        if i > 0:
            A = C[i] - C[i - 1]
            B = J[i] - J[i - 1]
            if A <= 0 and B <= 0:
                fail = True
                break
            elif B > 0 and A < 0:  # y/x > (-A)/B if B > 0
                if (-A) * q0 > p0 * B:
                    p0, q0 = -A, B
            elif B < 0 and A > 0:  # y/x < A/(-B) if B < 0
                if A * q1 < p1 * (-B):
                    p1, q1 = A, -B
    if fail or p0 * q1 >= p1 * q0:
        return "IMPOSSIBLE"
    p, q = middle(p0, q0, p1, q1)
    return str(p) + " " + str(q)

    Linear Fractional Transformations

    Another important concept related to continued fractions is the so-called linear fractional transformation.

    Linear fractional transformation

    A linear fractional transformation (or Möbius transformation) is a function 𝐿 :𝐑 →𝐑L:R→R such that

    𝐿(𝑥)=𝑎𝑥+𝑏𝑐𝑥+𝑑,L(x)=ax+bcx+d,

    where 𝑎,𝑏,𝑐,𝑑 ∈𝐑a,b,c,d∈R and 𝑎𝑑 −𝑏𝑐 ≠0ad−bc≠0.

    About the condition 𝑎𝑑 −𝑏𝑐 ≠0ad−bc≠0

    It is easy to verify that when 𝑎𝑑 −𝑏𝑐 =0ad−bc=0, the function may be undefined or a constant function.

    Linear fractional transformations have the following properties:

    Properties of linear fractional transformations

    Let 𝐿1,𝐿2,𝐿3L1,L2,L3 be linear fractional transformations, and denote the matrix formed by the coefficients of 𝐿𝑖Li as

    𝑀𝑖=(𝑎𝑖𝑏𝑖𝑐𝑖𝑑𝑖)Mi=(aibicidi)

    then they have the following properties:7

    1. The composition 𝐿1 ∘𝐿2L1∘L2 and inverse 𝐿−11L1−1 of linear fractional transformations are still linear fractional transformations, i.e., all linear fractional transformations form a group;
    2. Linear fractional transformations remain unchanged when their coefficients are multiplied by a non-zero constant, i.e., for any 𝜆 ≠0λ≠0, if 𝑀2 =𝜆𝑀1M2=λM1, then 𝐿2 =𝐿1L2=L1;
    3. The coefficient matrix of the composition of linear fractional transformations corresponds to the product of the coefficient matrices, i.e., if 𝑀1𝑀2 =𝑀3M1M2=M3, then 𝐿1 ∘𝐿2 =𝐿3L1∘L2=L3;
    4. The coefficient matrix of the inverse of a linear fractional transformation corresponds to the inverse of the coefficient matrix, i.e., if 𝑀−11 =𝑀2M1−1=M2, then 𝐿−11 =𝐿2L1−1=L2.
    Proof

    This only provides the forms of the composition and inverse of linear fractional transformations. After obtaining these forms, all properties are easy to verify.

    The composition of linear fractional transformations 𝐿1L1 and 𝐿2L2:

    𝐿1∘𝐿2=𝑎1𝑎2𝑥+𝑏2𝑐2𝑥+𝑑2+𝑏1𝑐1𝑎2𝑥+𝑏2𝑐2𝑥+𝑑2+𝑑1=(𝑎1𝑎2+𝑏1𝑐2)𝑥+(𝑎1𝑏2+𝑏1𝑑2)(𝑐1𝑎2+𝑑1𝑐2)𝑥+(𝑐1𝑏2+𝑑1𝑑2).L1∘L2=a1a2x+b2c2x+d2+b1c1a2x+b2c2x+d2+d1=(a1a2+b1c2)x+(a1b2+b1d2)(c1a2+d1c2)x+(c1b2+d1d2).

    The inverse of the linear fractional transformation 𝐿1(𝑥)L1(x):

    𝑦=𝐿1(𝑥)=𝑎1𝑥+𝑏1𝑐1𝑥+𝑑1⟺𝑥=𝐿−11(𝑦)=𝑑1𝑦−𝑏1−𝑐1𝑦+𝑎1.y=L1(x)=a1x+b1c1x+d1⟺x=L1−1(y)=d1y−b1−c1y+a1.

    The finite continued fraction [𝑎0,𝑎1,⋯,𝑎𝑛][a0,a1,⋯,an] can be viewed as the result of composing a series of linear fractional transformations. Let

    𝐿𝑖(𝑥)=𝑎𝑖𝑥+1𝑥=[𝑎𝑖,𝑥].Li(x)=aix+1x=[ai,x].

    Then the finite continued fraction

    [𝑎0,𝑎1,⋯,𝑎𝑛]=𝐿0∘𝐿1∘⋯𝐿𝑛(∞).[a0,a1,⋯,an]=L0∘L1∘⋯Ln(∞).

    Among them, the value of the linear fractional transformation 𝐿(𝑥) =𝑎𝑥+𝑏𝑐𝑥+𝑑L(x)=ax+bcx+d at 𝑥 =∞x=∞ is 𝑎𝑐ac, which is the limit of the function as 𝑥 → ±∞x→±∞.

    For a general continued fraction, let the remainder of a real number 𝑥x be 𝑟𝑘+1rk+1, i.e., 𝑥 =[𝑎0,⋯,𝑎𝑘,𝑟𝑘+1]x=[a0,⋯,ak,rk+1], then we have

    𝑥=𝐿0∘𝐿1∘⋯𝐿𝑘(𝑟𝑘+1)=𝑝𝑘𝑟𝑘+1+𝑝𝑘−1𝑞𝑘𝑟𝑘+1+𝑞𝑘−1.x=L0∘L1∘⋯Lk(rk+1)=pkrk+1+pk−1qkrk+1+qk−1.

    This also gives the form of the linear fractional transformation 𝐿0 ∘𝐿1 ∘⋯ ∘𝐿𝑘L0∘L1∘⋯∘Lk.

    We can also verify this expression directly. Initially:

    𝑥=𝑥+00𝑥+1=𝑝−1𝑥+𝑝−2𝑞−1𝑥+𝑞−2.x=x+00x+1=p−1x+p−2q−1x+q−2.

    Subsequently, if 𝐿0 ∘𝐿1 ∘⋯ ∘𝐿𝑘−1L0∘L1∘⋯∘Lk−1 has the form

    𝑝𝑘−1𝑥+𝑝𝑘−2𝑞𝑘−1𝑥+𝑞𝑘−2pk−1x+pk−2qk−1x+qk−2

    then according to the composition formula for linear fractional transformations,

    𝐿0∘𝐿1∘⋯∘𝐿𝑘−1∘𝐿𝑘=(𝑝𝑘−1𝑎𝑘+𝑝𝑘−2)𝑥+𝑝𝑘−1(𝑞𝑘−1𝑎𝑘+𝑞𝑘−2)𝑥+𝑞𝑘−1=𝑝𝑘𝑥+𝑝𝑘−1𝑞𝑘𝑥+𝑞𝑘−1.L0∘L1∘⋯∘Lk−1∘Lk=(pk−1ak+pk−2)x+pk−1(qk−1ak+qk−2)x+qk−1=pkx+pk−1qkx+qk−1.

    This gives the above form by induction. Linear fractional transformations also provide another perspective on the recurrence formula and initial conditions.

    DMOPC '19 Contest 7 P4 - Bob and Continued Fractions

    Given an array of positive integers 𝑎1,⋯,𝑎𝑛a1,⋯,an and 𝑚m queries, each query gives 𝑙 ≤𝑟l≤r, and requires computing the value of [𝑎𝑙,⋯,𝑎𝑟][al,⋯,ar].

    Solution

    Understanding continued fractions as the evaluation of a composition of linear fractional transformations at 𝑥 =∞x=∞, we only need to be able to query the composition of a range of linear fractional transformations multiple times. Since each linear fractional transformation can be inverted, we can preprocess prefix sums and use the difference method for queries, with complexity 𝑂(𝑛 +𝑚)O(n+m); if modifications are needed, we can also use data structures like segment trees.

    #include <algorithm>
#include <iostream>
#include <tuple>
#include <vector>

constexpr int M = 1e9 + 7;

// FLTs. Essentially 2x2 matrix.
struct FracLinearTrans {
  int mat[4];

  FracLinearTrans() : mat{} {}

  FracLinearTrans(int x) : mat{x, 1, 1, 0} {}

  FracLinearTrans(int a, int b, int c, int d) : mat{a, b, c, d} {}

  FracLinearTrans operator*(const FracLinearTrans& rhs) const {
    return FracLinearTrans(
        ((long long)mat[0] * rhs.mat[0] + (long long)mat[1] * rhs.mat[2]) % M,
        ((long long)mat[0] * rhs.mat[1] + (long long)mat[1] * rhs.mat[3]) % M,
        ((long long)mat[2] * rhs.mat[0] + (long long)mat[3] * rhs.mat[2]) % M,
        ((long long)mat[2] * rhs.mat[1] + (long long)mat[3] * rhs.mat[3]) % M);
  }

  FracLinearTrans inv() const {
    return FracLinearTrans(mat[3], M - mat[1], M - mat[2], mat[0]);
  }
};

int main() {
  int n, q;
  std::cin >> n >> q;
  // Get prefix sum of FLTs.
  std::vector<FracLinearTrans> ps(1, {1, 0, 0, 1});
  ps.reserve(n + 1);
  for (int i = 1; i <= n; ++i) {
    int a;
    std::cin >> a;
    ps[i] = ps[i - 1] * FracLinearTrans(a);
  }
  // Query.
  for (; q; --q) {
    int l, r;
    std::cin >> l >> r;
    // Difference.
    auto res = ps[l - 1].inv() * ps[r];
    int u = res.mat[0], d = res.mat[2];
    // Correct signs.
    if (!(l & 1)) {
      if (u) u = M - u;
      if (d) d = M - d;
    }
    printf("%d %d\n", u, d);
  }
  return 0;
}

def mul(a, b):

        (a[0] * b[0] + a[1] * b[2]) % M,
        (a[0] * b[1] + a[1] * b[3]) % M,
        (a[2] * b[0] + a[3] * b[2]) % M,
        (a[2] * b[1] + a[3] * b[3]) % M,
    )

n, q = map(int, input().split())

# Get presum.
for a in map(int, input().split()):
    ps.append(mul(ps[-1], (a, 1, 1, 0)))
for _ in range(q):
    l, r = map(int, input().split())
    res = mul(inv(ps[l - 1]), ps[r])
    u, d = res[0], res[2]
    if l % 2 == 0:

    print(u, d)

    Arithmetic Operations on Continued Fractions

    Using linear fractional transformations, we can perform arithmetic operations on continued fractions. This algorithm was first proposed by Gosper.

    The cornerstone of the algorithm is computing the linear fractional transformation of continued fractions. This section uses finite continued fractions as examples, but since the algorithm only needs to read in a finite number of continued fraction terms for each output digit, it is also applicable to infinite continued fractions and can be computed to any precision. Combined with the continued fraction comparison algorithm from earlier, we can precisely compare real numbers of arbitrary precision.

    Linear fractional transformation of continued fractions

    Given a linear fractional transformation 𝐿(𝑥) =𝑎𝑥+𝑏𝑐𝑥+𝑑L(x)=ax+bcx+d and a continued fraction 𝛼 =[𝛼0,𝛼1,⋯,𝛼𝑛]α=[α0,α1,⋯,αn], find the continued fraction representation [𝛽0,𝛽1,⋯,𝛽𝑚][β0,β1,⋯,βm] of 𝛽 =𝐿(𝛼)β=L(α).

    Solution

    The basic idea is to determine the values of 𝛽𝑖βi one by one. Let

    𝐿𝛾(𝑥)=𝛾+1𝑥=𝛾𝑥+1𝑥.Lγ(x)=γ+1x=γx+1x.

    Since

    𝐿(𝛼)=𝐿∘𝐿𝛼0∘𝐿𝛼1∘⋯∘𝐿𝛼𝑛(∞),L(α)=L∘Lα0∘Lα1∘⋯∘Lαn(∞),

    we can compute the value of 𝐿(𝛼)L(α) by gradually composing 𝐿𝛼𝑘Lαk with 𝐿L. However, if we want to get the continued fraction representation of 𝐿(𝛼)L(α), we do not need to completely compute the value of 𝐿(𝛼)L(α) first and then find its continued fraction representation. We can determine the values of 𝛽0,𝛽1,⋯β0,β1,⋯ during the process of composing 𝐿𝛼𝑖Lαi.

    For example, suppose currently we have computed

    𝐿∘𝐿𝛼0∘𝐿𝛼1∘⋯∘𝐿𝛼𝑘(𝑥)=𝑎𝑘𝑥+𝑏𝑘𝑐𝑘𝑥+𝑑𝑘L∘Lα0∘Lα1∘⋯∘Lαk(x)=akx+bkckx+dk

    and 𝑐𝑘,𝑑𝑘ck,dk have the same sign. Then 𝐿 ∘𝐿𝛼0 ∘𝐿𝛼1 ∘⋯ ∘𝐿𝛼𝑘(𝑥)L∘Lα0∘Lα1∘⋯∘Lαk(x) is monotonic on [0,∞][0,∞], and its value must lie between 𝑎𝑘𝑐𝑘akck and 𝑏𝑘𝑑𝑘bkdk. So if

    ⌊𝑎𝑘𝑐𝑘⌋=⌊𝑏𝑘𝑑𝑘⌋,⌊akck⌋=⌊bkdk⌋,

    we can determine that it is the integer part 𝛽0β0 of 𝐿 ∘𝐿𝛼0 ∘𝐿𝛼1 ∘⋯ ∘𝐿𝛼𝑘(𝑥)L∘Lα0∘Lα1∘⋯∘Lαk(x). At this time, composing 𝐿−1𝛽0Lβ0−1 on the left gives

    𝐿−1𝛽0∘𝐿∘𝐿𝛼0∘𝐿𝛼1∘⋯∘𝐿𝛼𝑘.Lβ0−1∘L∘Lα0∘Lα1∘⋯∘Lαk.

    Then we can continue adding 𝐿𝛼𝑘+1,𝐿𝛼𝑘+2,⋯Lαk+1,Lαk+2,⋯ to determine the new integer part, i.e., 𝛽1β1. Continue this process until all 𝛽𝑗βj are determined.

    The algorithm requires 𝑐c and 𝑑d to have the same sign to ensure that the discontinuity point of the function is not in [0,∞][0,∞]. This is always possible because the definition of simple continued fractions requires that all coefficients (except 𝛼0α0) are positive integers. From this, it can be proved that 𝑐c and 𝑑d will eventually have the same sign in finite steps and will continue to have the same sign thereafter.

    In actual implementation, we only need to maintain the coefficient matrix (𝑎𝑏𝑐𝑑)(abcd) of the current linear fractional transformation and check whether 𝑐c and 𝑑d have the same sign and whether 𝑎𝑐ac and 𝑏𝑑bd have the same integer part. When composing 𝐿𝛼𝑖Lαi on the right, we get (𝑎𝛼𝑖+𝑏𝑎𝑐𝛼𝑖+𝑑𝑐)(aαi+bacαi+dc). If both integer parts are the same as 𝛽𝑗βj, then we add 𝛽𝑗βj to the continued fraction, and compose 𝐿−1𝛽𝑗Lβj−1 on the left, which is equivalent to computing (𝑐𝑑𝑎mod𝑐𝑏mod𝑑)(cdamodcbmodd).

    The linear fractional transformation of continued fractions can already be used to compute the arithmetic operations of fractions and continued fractions:

    𝑝𝑞±𝑥=±𝑞𝑥+𝑝0𝑥+𝑞, 𝑝𝑞𝑥=𝑝𝑥+00𝑥+𝑞, 𝑝𝑞/𝑥=0𝑥+𝑝𝑞𝑥+0.pq±x=±qx+p0x+q, pqx=px+00x+q, pq/x=0x+pqx+0.

    For general arithmetic operations between continued fractions, we need to use bilinear fractional transformations:

    𝑥+𝑦=0𝑥𝑦+𝑥+𝑦+00𝑥𝑦+0𝑥+0𝑦+1, 𝑥𝑦=1𝑥𝑦+0𝑥+0𝑦+00𝑥𝑦+0𝑥+0𝑦+1, 𝑥𝑦=0𝑥𝑦+𝑥+0𝑦+00𝑥𝑦+0𝑥+𝑦+0.x+y=0xy+x+y+00xy+0x+0y+1, xy=1xy+0x+0y+00xy+0x+0y+1, xy=0xy+x+0y+00xy+0x+y+0.
    Bilinear fractional transformation of continued fractions

    Given a bilinear fractional transformation 𝐿(𝑥,𝑦) =𝑎𝑥𝑦+𝑏𝑥+𝑐𝑦+𝑑𝑒𝑥𝑦+𝑓𝑥+𝑔𝑦+ℎL(x,y)=axy+bx+cy+dexy+fx+gy+h and continued fractions 𝛼 =[𝛼0,𝛼1,⋯,𝛼𝑛]α=[α0,α1,⋯,αn] and 𝛽 =[𝛽0,𝛽1,⋯,𝛽𝑚]β=[β0,β1,⋯,βm], find the continued fraction representation [𝛾0,𝛾1,⋯,𝛾ℓ][γ0,γ1,⋯,γℓ] of 𝛾 =𝐿(𝛼,𝛽)γ=L(α,β).

    Solution

    Similar to the case of single-variable linear fractional transformations, to determine the integer part, we only need to ensure that the integer part of the current bilinear fractional transformation remains unchanged in (𝑥,𝑦) ∈[0,∞] ×[0,∞](x,y)∈[0,∞]×[0,∞], i.e., 𝑒,𝑓,𝑔,ℎe,f,g,h all have the same sign, and

    ⌊𝑎𝑒⌋=⌊𝑏𝑓⌋=⌊𝑐𝑔⌋=⌊𝑑ℎ⌋.⌊ae⌋=⌊bf⌋=⌊cg⌋=⌊dh⌋.

    Right composition is replaced by computing 𝐿(𝑥,𝑦) ↦𝐿(𝐿𝛼𝑖(𝑥),𝑦)L(x,y)↦L(Lαi(x),y) and 𝐿(𝑥,𝑦) ↦𝐿(𝑥,𝐿𝛽𝑗(𝑦))L(x,y)↦L(x,Lβj(y)), which are also represented as linear transformations of coefficients. Left composition is completely consistent with the single-variable case, we only need to compute the modulo.

    Compared to the single-variable case, the two-variable case needs to decide whether to compose 𝐿𝛼𝑖Lαi or 𝐿𝛽𝑗Lβj first. Since the order of composition does not affect the final result, we can freely choose the order of composition, such as alternately composing 𝐿𝛼𝑖Lαi and 𝐿𝛽𝑗Lβj. Or using the empirical rule, prioritize the dimension with the larger ratio difference: if ∣𝑏𝑓−𝑑ℎ∣ >∣𝑐𝑔−𝑑ℎ∣|bf−dh|>|cg−dh|, then first compose 𝐿𝛼𝑖Lαi; otherwise, first compose 𝐿𝛽𝑗Lβj.

    Periodic Continued Fractions

    Similar to the concept of repeating decimals, if the coefficients of a continued fraction form a cycle, it is called a periodic continued fraction.

    Periodic continued fraction

    Let the continued fraction 𝑥 =[𝑎0,𝑎1,𝑎2,⋯]x=[a0,a1,a2,⋯], and there exist natural numbers 𝐾K and positive integer 𝐿L such that for any 𝑘 ≥𝐾k≥K, we have 𝑎𝑘 =𝑎𝑘+𝐿ak=ak+L, then 𝑥x is called a periodic continued fraction. The smallest 𝐿L satisfying this condition is called its minimal positive period, and the sequence 𝑎𝑘,⋯,𝑎𝑘+𝐿−1ak,⋯,ak+L−1 that repeats in the continued fraction is called its repeating block. Using the repeating block, the periodic continued fraction can be written as 𝑥 =[𝑎0,⋯,𝑎𝑘−1,―――――――𝑎𝑘,⋯,𝑎𝑘+𝐿−1]x=[a0,⋯,ak−1,ak,⋯,ak+L−1―]. If 𝐾K can be taken as 00, i.e., 𝑥 =[――――――𝑎0,⋯,𝑎𝐿−1]x=[a0,⋯,aL−1―], then it is called a purely periodic continued fraction, otherwise it is called a mixed periodic continued fraction.

    Quadratic Irrationals

    The concept closely related to periodic continued fractions is the (real) quadratic irrational, i.e., the irrational solutions of quadratic equations with integer coefficients. All quadratic irrationals can be expressed in the form

    𝑎+𝑏√𝐷a+bD

    where 𝑎,𝑏a,b are rational numbers and 𝐷D is a positive integer without square factors. The quadratic irrationals mentioned in this article are all assumed to be real numbers. Moreover, the conjugate of 𝑎 +𝑏√𝐷a+bD is 𝑎 −𝑏√𝐷a−bD.

    Euler's result shows that all periodic continued fractions are quadratic irrationals.

    Theorem (Euler)

    Periodic continued fractions all represent quadratic irrationals.

    Proof

    For a general periodic continued fraction 𝑥 =[𝑎0,⋯,𝑎𝑘−1,―――――――𝑎𝑘,⋯,𝑎𝑘+𝐿−1]x=[a0,⋯,ak−1,ak,⋯,ak+L−1―], we can set 𝑦 =[―――――――𝑎𝑘,⋯,𝑎𝑘+𝐿−1]y=[ak,⋯,ak+L−1―], then

    𝑥=[𝑎0,⋯,𝑎𝑘−1,𝑦]=𝐿0(𝑦),𝑦=[𝑎𝑘,⋯,𝑎𝑘+𝐿−1,𝑦]=𝐿1(𝑦),x=[a0,⋯,ak−1,y]=L0(y),y=[ak,⋯,ak+L−1,y]=L1(y),

    where both 𝐿0( ⋅)L0(⋅) and 𝐿1( ⋅)L1(⋅) are linear fractional transformations. Thus, the equation satisfied by 𝑥x is

    𝑥=𝐿0∘𝐿1∘𝐿−10(𝑥).x=L0∘L1∘L0−1(x).

    Let the linear fractional transformation 𝐿0 ∘𝐿1 ∘𝐿−10(𝑥) =𝑎𝑥+𝑏𝑐𝑥+𝑑L0∘L1∘L0−1(x)=ax+bcx+d, then we get the equation satisfied by 𝑥x

    𝑐𝑥2+(𝑑−𝑎)𝑥−𝑏=0.cx2+(d−a)x−b=0.

    Therefore, periodic continued fractions are all solutions of quadratic equations with integer coefficients. Moreover, since infinite continued fractions are all irrational numbers, periodic continued fractions all represent quadratic irrationals.

    Lagrange's result shows the converse also holds, so quadratic irrationals and periodic continued fractions are equivalent.

    Theorem (Lagrange)

    Quadratic irrationals can be expressed as periodic continued fractions.

    Proof

    The idea is to prove that remainders repeat. Let a quadratic irrational 𝑥x be written in the form

    𝑥=𝑃0+√𝐷𝑄0x=P0+DQ0

    where 𝑃0,𝑄0,𝐷P0,Q0,D are all integers and 𝑄0 ∣𝐷 −𝑃20Q0∣D−P02. This is always possible, for example, a quadratic irrational 𝑥x can always be written as

    𝑎+𝑏√𝐷′=𝑝𝑎𝑞𝑎+𝑝𝑏𝑞𝑏√𝐷′=𝑝𝑎𝑞𝑏+𝑝𝑏𝑞𝑎√𝐷′𝑞𝑎𝑞𝑏=𝑝𝑎𝑝𝑏𝑞𝑎𝑞𝑏+√(𝑞𝑎𝑞𝑏)2𝐷′(𝑞𝑎𝑞𝑏)2a+bD′=paqa+pbqbD′=paqb+pbqaD′qaqb=papbqaqb+(qaqb)2D′(qaqb)2

    then let 𝑃 =𝑝𝑎𝑝𝑏𝑞𝑎𝑞𝑏P=papbqaqb, 𝑄 =(𝑞𝑎𝑞𝑏)2Q=(qaqb)2 and 𝐷 =𝑄𝐷′D=QD′.

    The benefit of writing it in this form is that we can prove all its remainders have a similar form:

    𝑟𝑘=𝑃𝑘+√𝐷𝑄𝑘,rk=Pk+DQk,

    where 𝑃𝑘,𝑄𝑘Pk,Qk are integers and 𝑄𝑘 ∣𝐷 −𝑃2𝑘Qk∣D−Pk2. Here, the condition 𝑄𝑘 ∣𝐷 −𝑃2𝑘Qk∣D−Pk2 ensures that the coefficient in front of √𝐷D in the numerator of all remainders is 11.

    To get the form of the remainder, we can use mathematical induction. When 𝑘 =0k=0, it is obvious. Assuming we have obtained the form of 𝑟𝑘rk, and let 𝑎𝑘 =⌊𝑟𝑘⌋ak=⌊rk⌋, then

    𝑟𝑘=𝑎𝑘+1𝑟𝑘+1.rk=ak+1rk+1.

    Assume 𝑟𝑘+1rk+1 also has a similar form, and substitute together with 𝑟𝑘rk into the above equation:

    𝑃𝑘+√𝐷𝑄𝑘=𝑎𝑘+𝑄𝑘+1𝑃𝑘+1+√𝐷=𝑎𝑘+𝑄𝑘+1𝑃𝑘+1−𝑄𝑘+1√𝐷𝑃2𝑘+1−𝐷.Pk+DQk=ak+Qk+1Pk+1+D=ak+Qk+1Pk+1−Qk+1DPk+12−D.

    Since expressing quadratic irrationals as 𝑎 +𝑏√𝐷a+bD is unique, comparing coefficients on both sides, we get

    𝑃𝑘𝑄𝑘=𝑎𝑘+𝑄𝑘+1𝑃𝑘+1𝑃2𝑘+1−𝐷, 1𝑄𝑘=−𝑄𝑘+1𝑃2𝑘+1−𝐷.PkQk=ak+Qk+1Pk+1Pk+12−D, 1Qk=−Qk+1Pk+12−D.

    Substituting the second equation into the first equation, we can solve for 𝑃𝑘+1Pk+1:

    𝑃𝑘𝑄𝑘=𝑎𝑘−𝑃𝑘+1𝑄𝑘⟺𝑃𝑘+1=𝑎𝑘𝑄𝑘−𝑃𝑘.PkQk=ak−Pk+1Qk⟺Pk+1=akQk−Pk.

    Substituting into the second equation, we can solve for 𝑄𝑘+1Qk+1:

    𝑄𝑘+1=𝐷−𝑃2𝑘+1𝑄𝑘=𝐷−(𝑎𝑘𝑄𝑘−𝑃𝑘)2𝑄𝑘=−𝑎2𝑘𝑄𝑘+2𝑎𝑘𝑃𝑘+𝐷−𝑃2𝑘𝑄𝑘.Qk+1=D−Pk+12Qk=D−(akQk−Pk)2Qk=−ak2Qk+2akPk+D−Pk2Qk.

    According to the induction hypothesis, 𝑄𝑘 ∣𝐷 −𝑃2𝑘Qk∣D−Pk2, so indeed both 𝑃𝑘+1Pk+1 and 𝑄𝑘+1Qk+1 are integers, i.e., 𝑟𝑘+1rk+1 also has the required form.

    Finally, we prove that remainders can only take finitely many values, so they must repeat. We have obtained the remainder earlier

    𝑃𝑘+√𝐷𝑄𝑘=𝑟𝑘=−𝑞𝑘−2𝑥−𝑝𝑘−2𝑞𝑘−1𝑥−𝑝𝑘−1Pk+DQk=rk=−qk−2x−pk−2qk−1x−pk−1

    and for irrational numbers, we always have 𝑟𝑘 >1rk>1. At the same time, its conjugate

    𝑃𝑘−√𝐷𝑄𝑘=𝑟∗𝑘=−𝑞𝑘−2𝑥∗−𝑝𝑘−2𝑞𝑘−1𝑥∗−𝑝𝑘−1=−𝑞𝑘−2𝑞𝑘−1𝑥∗−𝑝𝑘−2𝑞𝑘−2𝑥∗−𝑝𝑘−1𝑞𝑘−1Pk−DQk=rk∗=−qk−2x∗−pk−2qk−1x∗−pk−1=−qk−2qk−1x∗−pk−2qk−2x∗−pk−1qk−1

    must be less than 00 for sufficiently large 𝑘k, because

    𝑞𝑘−2𝑞𝑘−1>0, lim𝑘→∞𝑥∗−𝑝𝑘−2𝑞𝑘−2𝑥∗−𝑝𝑘−1𝑞𝑘−1=𝑥∗−𝑥𝑥∗−𝑥=1.qk−2qk−1>0, limk→∞x∗−pk−2qk−2x∗−pk−1qk−1=x∗−xx∗−x=1.

    This shows that

    2√𝐷𝑄𝑘=𝑟𝑘−𝑟∗𝑘>1⟺0<𝑄𝑘≤2√𝐷.2DQk=rk−rk∗>1⟺0<Qk≤2D.

    Therefore, 𝑄𝑘Qk can only take finitely many values. Furthermore,

    𝐷−𝑃2𝑘=𝑄𝑘𝑄𝑘−1>0⟺|𝑃𝑘|<√𝐷,D−Pk2=QkQk−1>0⟺|Pk|<D,

    so 𝑃𝑘Pk can also only take finitely many values. Hence, the remainder 𝑟𝑘rk has only finitely many possible values and must repeat within infinite terms.

    The proof of this theorem also provides a recurrence formula for computing the remainders of quadratic irrationals:

    Recurrence formula for quadratic irrationals

    A quadratic irrational can always be expressed in the form

    𝑥=𝑃0+√𝐷𝑄0x=P0+DQ0

    with 𝑄0 ∣𝐷 −𝑃20Q0∣D−P02. Its remainder

    𝑟𝑘=𝑃𝑘+√𝐷𝑄𝑘rk=Pk+DQk

    where 𝑃𝑘,𝑄𝑘Pk,Qk are all integers, and satisfy the recurrence relations

    𝑃𝑘+1=𝑎𝑘𝑄𝑘−𝑃𝑘,𝑄𝑘+1=𝐷−𝑃2𝑘+1𝑄𝑘.Pk+1=akQk−Pk,Qk+1=D−Pk+12Qk.

    This recurrence formula can be directly used for the continued fraction computation of quadratic irrationals, and according to the proof of the theorem, |𝑃𝑘| <√𝐷|Pk|<D and 𝑄𝑘 ≤2√𝐷Qk≤2D. The complexity of this algorithm depends on the length of the repeating block, and the latter can be proved to be 𝑂(√𝐷log⁡𝐷)O(Dlog⁡D)2.

    Quadratic irrationals

    Given a quadratic irrational 𝛼 =𝑥+𝑦√𝑛𝑧α=x+ynz, find its continued fraction representation. Here, 𝑥,𝑦,𝑧,𝑛 ∈𝐙x,y,z,n∈Z and 𝑛 >0n>0 is not a perfect square.

    Solution

    First express the quadratic irrational in the above form, then use the recurrence formula to compute it. The terms of the continued fraction are given by 𝑎𝑘 =⌊𝑟𝑘⌋ak=⌊rk⌋. To find the repeating block, we need to store the indices where (𝑃𝑘,𝑄𝑘)(Pk,Qk) first appear.

    // Return the continued fraction and minimal positive period
//   of a quadratic irrational (x + y * sqrt(n)) / z.
auto quadratic_irrational(int x, int y, int z, int n) {
  int p = x * z;
  int d = n * y * y * z * z;
  int q = z * z;
  int dd = (int)sqrt(n) * y * z;
  int i = 0;
  std::vector<int> a;
  std::unordered_map<size_t, int> used;
  while (!used.count(((1LL << 32) * p) | q)) {
    a.emplace_back((p + dd) / q);
    used[((1LL << 32) * p) | q] = i++;
    p = a.back() * q - p;
    q = (d - p * p) / q;
  }
  return std::make_pair(a, i - used[((1LL << 32) * p) | q]);
}

    # Return the continued fraction and minimal positive period
#   of a quadratic irrational (x + y * sqrt(n)) / z.
def quadratic_irrational(x, y, z, n):
    p = x * z
    d = n * y * y * z * z
    q = z * z
    dd = floor(sqrt(n)) * y * z
    i = 0
    a = []
    used = dict()
    while (p, q) not in used:
        a.append((p + dd) // q)
        used[p, q] = i
        p = a[-1] * q - p
        q = (d - p * p) // q
        i += 1
    return a, i - used[p, q]
    Tavrida NU Akai Contest - Continued Fraction

    Given 𝑥x and 𝑘k, where 𝑥x is not a perfect square, 0 ≤𝑘 ≤1090≤k≤109. Find the 𝑘k-th convergent 𝑥𝑘xk of √𝑥x.

    Solution

    First use the above algorithm to find the period of √𝑥x, express the repeating block as a linear fractional transformation, and then use fast exponentiation to obtain the value of 𝑥𝑘xk. Of course, for parts that have not entered the repeating block or are less than one repeating block, they need to be handled separately.

    #include <algorithm>
#include <cmath>
#include <iostream>
#include <tuple>
#include <unordered_map>
#include <vector>

// Return the continued fraction and minimal positive period
//   of a quadratic irrational (x + y * sqrt(n)) / z.
auto quadratic_irrational(int x, int y, int z, int n) {
  int p = x * z;
  int d = n * y * y * z * z;
  int q = z * z;
  int dd = (int)sqrt(n) * y * z;
  int i = 0;
  std::vector<int> a;
  std::unordered_map<size_t, int> used;
  while (!used.count(((1LL << 32) * p) | q)) {
    a.emplace_back((p + dd) / q);
    used[((1LL << 32) * p) | q] = i++;
    p = a.back() * q - p;
    q = (d - p * p) / q;
  }
  return std::make_pair(a, i - used[((1LL << 32) * p) | q]);
}

// Fractional Linear Transformation.
struct FracLinearTrans {
  static constexpr int M = 1e9 + 7;
  int mat[4];

  FracLinearTrans(int a, int b, int c, int d) : mat{a, b, c, d} {}

  FracLinearTrans operator*(const FracLinearTrans& rhs) const {
    return FracLinearTrans(
        ((long long)mat[0] * rhs.mat[0] + (long long)mat[1] * rhs.mat[2]) % M,
        ((long long)mat[0] * rhs.mat[1] + (long long)mat[1] * rhs.mat[3]) % M,
        ((long long)mat[2] * rhs.mat[0] + (long long)mat[3] * rhs.mat[2]) % M,
        ((long long)mat[2] * rhs.mat[1] + (long long)mat[3] * rhs.mat[3]) % M);
  }
};

int main() {
  int x, k, L;
  std::cin >> x >> k;
  std::vector<int> a;
  std::tie(a, L) =
      quadratic_irrational(0, 1, 1, x);  // L==a.size()-1 for sqrt(x)
  FracLinearTrans cyc(1, 0, 0, 1);
  for (int i = a.size() - 1; i; --i) {
    cyc = FracLinearTrans(a[i], 1, 1, 0) * cyc;
  }
  // 1/0=Inf.
  FracLinearTrans res(0, 1, 0, 0);
  // Tail terms.
  for (int i = k % L; i; --i) {
    res = FracLinearTrans(a[i], 1, 1, 0) * res;
  }
  // Binary exponentiation.
  for (int b = k / L; b; b >>= 1) {
    if (b & 1) res = cyc * res;
    cyc = cyc * cyc;
  }
  // First term.
  res = FracLinearTrans(a[0], 1, 1, 0) * res;
  printf("%d/%d", res.mat[1], res.mat[3]);
  return 0;
}
